The letter \(\varepsilon\) has three meanings in the book, which we tell apart by the notation: \(\varepsilon(x)\) is the strain of a bar at the point \(x\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is an entry of the tensor, and \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) is the strain of a short fibre in the direction \(\vek n\). All of them tell by how much something gets longer compared with its length, but they are different objects. For the diagonal \(AC\) of the cube, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005\) is an entry of the tensor and \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) is the strain of the diagonal.

What remains of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre? We denote the strain of a short fibre in the direction \(\vek n\), that is, the limit (1.50), by \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\). The vector in the brackets reminds us that this is a strain in a direction, not the strain \(\varepsilon(x)\) of a bar at the point \(x\). The theorem gives it when \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is not the zero vector, and for small partial derivatives this always holds, as we show in step 8. Let us show in steps how \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) differs from the double sum with the matrix \(\ten\varepsilon\).

The steps below point to three figures. The first shows the displacement of the end of the fibre. We denote \(\vek w = \mat H\,\vek n\), which is the displacement of the end divided by \(h\) (explanation in step 5).

The point \(P\) is the start of the fibre, drawn relative to \(P\), that is, without the common displacement \(\vek u(P)\). The blackwhite segment to \(Q\) is the fibre \(h\,\vek n\) before loading. The orange segment from \(P\) to \(Q_1\) is the same fibre after loading, of length \(L_1\). We do not draw the remainders and everything is greatly magnified. The blue dimension from \(Q\) to \(Q_1\) is the displacement of the end, \(h\,\vek w\). We split it into two perpendicular parts. The part along the fibre has length \(h\,t\), where \(t\) is the component of the vector \(\vek w\) in the direction \(\vek n\), and shows the lengthening of the fibre. The part across it has length \(h\,p\), where \(p\) is the length of the part of the vector \(\vek w\) perpendicular to \(\vek n\), and the right angle between them shows that they are perpendicular. The bottom dimension has length \((1 + t)\,h\), that is, the fibre together with the longitudinal part of the displacement. This dimension and the transverse part are the legs of a right triangle, and the fibre after loading is its hypotenuse. So it is never shorter than \((1 + t)\,h\).

The second figure shows the inequality that we use in step 6.

Let us draw why this holds, on the made-up numbers \(b = 0{,}7\) and \(d = 0{,}3\). The large square has the side \(b + d\), which is made of the length \(b\) and the length \(d\). The two blue squares in opposite corners have the areas \(b^2\) and \(d^2\). The two grey rectangles each have the area \(b\,d\), together \(2bd\). The two blue squares together cover more area than the two grey rectangles, by \((b - d)^2\), which is not negative. On the right this difference is shown: the square with the side \(b\) is covered by two grey rectangles \(b \times d\), along the left and the bottom edge, and they overlap in the square \(d^2\) (darker). The covered area is \(2bd - d^2\), and what remains uncovered is the square with the side \(b - d\), with the area \(b^2 - 2bd + d^2 = (b - d)^2\).

The third figure is the chain of estimates from steps 6 to 9, on an example with \(m = 0{,}1\), where \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the first column of the matrix \(\mat H\) is \((0, m, m)\) and all other entries are zero, so that \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m\) and \(\vek w = (0, m, m)\). Row (6): the blue segment is \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| + |n_{\mathrm{y}}| + |n_{\mathrm{z}}| = 1\) and the grey one is the bound \(\sqrt3\). Row (7): the length \(|\vek w| = \sqrt2\,m \approx 0{,}141\) is below the bound \(3m = 0{,}3\). Row (8): the number \(t\) is zero here, because \(\vek w\) is perpendicular to \(\vek n\), and the strain \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = \sqrt{1{,}02} - 1 \approx 0{,}00995\) is above it, as \(\varepsilon(\vek n) \ge t\) requires. Row (9), in units of \(m^2 = 0{,}01\): the difference \(\varepsilon(\vek n) - t = 0{,}995\,m^2\) is below half the square \(\tfrac12|\vek w|^2 = 1{,}0\,m^2\), and this is below the bound \(4{,}5\,m^2\).

  1. From (1.50) it follows that \(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n) = \sqrt{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n}\). We square and multiply out \((1 + \varepsilon(\vek n))^2 = 1 + 2\varepsilon(\vek n) + \varepsilon(\vek n)^2\). Subtracting \(1\) and dividing by \(2\) gives exactly

    \[\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n = \varepsilon(\vek n) + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 .\]

  2. We substitute \(\mat E = \ten\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\). A double sum with a sum of matrices is the sum of the double sums, because every term \(n_{\mathrm{j}}\,(A_{\mathrm{jk}} + B_{\mathrm{jk}})\,n_{\mathrm{k}}\) splits into two. So \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + \tfrac12\,\vek n^\T\mat H^\T\mat H\,\vek n\).

  3. The double sum \(\vek n^\T\mat H^\T\mat H\,\vek n\) is the square of the length of the vector \(\mat H\,\vek n\), \(|\mat H\,\vek n|^2\). The same steps 2 to 5 as for \(|\mat F\,\vek n|^2\) before definition 1.112 show this, only with \(\mat H\) instead of \(\mat F\):

    \[\vek n^\T\mat H^\T\mat H\,\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\Big)^2 = |\mat H\,\vek n|^2 .\]

  4. Steps 1 to 3 give the exact equality

    \[\varepsilon(\vek n) = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + \tfrac12\,|\mat H\,\vek n|^2 - \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 .\]

  5. The two corrections on the right are halves of squares of two numbers, the strain \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) and the length \(|\mat H\,\vek n|\). What does the vector \(\mat H\,\vek n\) measure? By lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading, the difference of the displacements of the ends of the fibre equals, up to the remainders, \(\mat H\,(h\,\vek n) = h\,\mat H\,\vek n\). So the vector \(\mat H\,\vek n\) is the displacement of the end \(Q\) relative to the start \(P\), divided by \(h\). We denote it by \(\vek w = \mat H\,\vek n\). In figure 1.394, \(h\,\vek w\) is the blue displacement of the end. We will bound the length \(|\vek w|\) by the number \(m\) from the small deformation assumption (step 7). We will not bound the strain \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\): in step 8 we compare it with the number \(t\), which is the length of the part of the displacement \(\vek w\) along the fibre, divided by \(h\) (figure 1.394), and in step 9 the correction \(-\tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2\) drops out, because it is not positive.

  6. First we bound the sum of the absolute values of the components of the unit vector \(\vek n\). For nonnegative numbers \(b\) and \(d\) we have \(2bd \le b^2 + d^2\), because the difference \(b^2 + d^2 - 2bd = (b - d)^2\) is a square and therefore not negative. We use this for all three pairs of numbers \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}|\), \(|n_{\mathrm{y}}|\) and \(|n_{\mathrm{z}}|\), whose squares are \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2\), \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\):

    \[\begin{aligned} \big(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| + |n_{\mathrm{y}}| + |n_{\mathrm{z}}|\big)^2 &= n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 2|n_{\mathrm{x}}|\,|n_{\mathrm{y}}| + 2|n_{\mathrm{x}}|\,|n_{\mathrm{z}}| + 2|n_{\mathrm{y}}|\,|n_{\mathrm{z}}| \\ &\le 1 + (n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2) + (n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2) + (n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2) = 1 + 2 = 3 . \end{aligned}\]

    By lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, it follows that \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| + |n_{\mathrm{y}}| + |n_{\mathrm{z}}| \le \sqrt3\).

  7. The length of the vector \(\vek w\). Its component \(\ix{i}\) is \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\). By the triangle inequality for numbers and the rule for the absolute value of a product (lemma 1.6) and by step 6,

    \[|w_{\mathrm{i}}| \le \sum_{\mathrm{j}} |H_{\mathrm{ij}}|\,|n_{\mathrm{j}}| \le m\,\big(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| + |n_{\mathrm{y}}| + |n_{\mathrm{z}}|\big) \le \sqrt3\,m .\]

    So \(|\vek w|^2 = w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{z}}^2 \le 3 \cdot 3m^2 = 9m^2\), by lemma 1.28 \(|\vek w| \le 3m\), and the first correction is at most \(\tfrac12 \cdot 9m^2 = 4{,}5\,m^2\). The factor \(3\) cannot be reduced. If all entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) equal \(m\) and \(\vek n = (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3\), each component of the vector \(\vek w\) is a sum of three equal products, \(3 \cdot m/\sqrt3 = \sqrt3\,m\), and \(|\vek w| = \sqrt{3 \cdot 3m^2} = 3m\). For \(m = 0{,}001\) the end of the fibre can therefore move relative to \(P\) by \(0{,}003\) of the length of the fibre, three times the largest partial derivative.

  8. The strain of the fibre. We write the vector \(\vek w\) as the sum \(t\,\vek n + (\vek w - t\,\vek n)\), where \(t = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,w_{\mathrm{i}}\). The first part is the part of the displacement along the fibre, the second the part across it, and we denote the square of the length of the second part by \(p^2\). Since \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = 1\),

    \[p^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} (w_{\mathrm{i}} - t\,n_{\mathrm{i}})^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - 2t \sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,w_{\mathrm{i}} + t^2 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = |\vek w|^2 - t^2 .\]

    The sum of squares \(p^2\) is not negative, so \(t^2 \le |\vek w|^2\) and by lemma 1.28 \(|t| \le |\vek w| \le 3m\). We write the square of the length of the vector \(\mat F\,\vek n = \vek n + \vek w\) component by component, as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 1.114:

    \[|\mat F\,\vek n|^2 = 1 + 2t + |\vek w|^2 = 1 + 2t + t^2 + p^2 = (1 + t)^2 + p^2 .\]

    So the fibre after loading is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the leg \((1 + t)\,h\) along the original direction and the transverse leg \(p\,h\). For \(m < \tfrac13\) we have \(1 + t \ge 1 - 3m > 0\). So \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is not the zero vector, item 2 of the theorem holds, and by its proof \(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n) = |\mat F\,\vek n|\). Since \(|\mat F\,\vek n|^2 \ge (1 + t)^2\) and the numbers \(|\mat F\,\vek n|\) and \(1 + t\) are positive, by lemma 1.28 \(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n) \ge 1 + t\), so \(\varepsilon(\vek n) \ge t\).

  9. The number \(t\) is the double sum with the matrix \(\ten\varepsilon\). We have \(t = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\), and this sum does not change if we replace \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) by \(H_{\mathrm{ji}}\), because that only renames the indices. So \(t = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}})\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\). The formula with the small strain tensor therefore takes only the part of the displacement of the end along the fibre. From step 8 and the equality in step 4 it follows that

    \[0 \le \varepsilon(\vek n) - \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \tfrac12\,|\vek w|^2 - \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 \le \tfrac12\,|\vek w|^2 \le 4{,}5\,m^2 .\]

    So the small strain tensor never overestimates the strain of a fibre, and underestimates it by at most \(4{,}5\,m^2\). It underestimates it because the transverse part of the displacement tilts the fibre and lengthens it a little in doing so, as the hypotenuse is longer than the leg. In the example of step 7 there is no transverse part, because \(\vek w = 3m\,\vek n\), and there is no error. The error is large when the displacement of the end is mostly transverse, as for the vertical edge \(AD\) below. The estimate needs exactly the small deformation assumption with \(m < \tfrac13\). When the partial derivatives are not small, the error can be large, as we will see in section 1.17.6. We leave out the corrections:

    \[\varepsilon(\vek n) \approx \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} .\]

  10. We write out the double sum. The terms with \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) give \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\). The terms with \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\) come in pairs, for example \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\), which are equal because \(\ten\varepsilon\) is symmetric. Each pair gives twice one term:

    \[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon(\vek n) &\approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 \\ &\quad + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned} \tag{1.53}\]

This is the formula we will use most often. We need it whenever we care about stretching in a direction that is not an axis, for example along the diagonal of a cube or along a slanted fibre of a bar. From six numbers at the point \(P\) it gives the strain of a short fibre in every direction through \(P\), with no roots and no products of partial derivatives (CM (3.5.6), PDF p. 142, BOWER, PDF p. 50, SADD (2.3.3), PDF p. 47). Let us test it on our fibres.

  • The diagonal \(AC\) of the sheared cube, \(\vek n = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\): the formula gives \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = 2 \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot \tfrac12 = 0{,}0005\), the exact strain is \(5{,}0012 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The corrections of step 4 are \(\tfrac12|\mat H\,\vek n|^2 = 2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) and \(-\tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 = -1{,}25 \cdot 10^{-7}\), and their sum \(1{,}25 \cdot 10^{-7}\) is exactly the difference.
  • The fibre from the point \(P\) of the hanging bar in the direction \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\): the formula gives
    \[\begin{aligned} &1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot \tfrac19 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot \tfrac49 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot \tfrac49 \\ &\qquad = 2{,}168889 \cdot 10^{-7} - 5{,}205333 \cdot 10^{-7} = -3{,}036444 \cdot 10^{-7} , \end{aligned}\]
    the exact strain \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = \sqrt{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n} - 1\) is \(-3{,}036441 \cdot 10^{-7}\). On the digits shown they differ by \(3 \cdot 10^{-13}\). We get the difference more precisely from the corrections of step 4. We computed the vector \(\mat H\,\vek n = (6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-7},\ -3{,}9024 \cdot 10^{-7},\ -3{,}9040 \cdot 10^{-7})\) in section 1.16.2, so
    \[\tfrac12\,|\mat H\,\vek n|^2 - \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 = 3{,}638 \cdot 10^{-13} - 0{,}461 \cdot 10^{-13} = 3{,}2 \cdot 10^{-13} ,\]
    almost a million times less than the strain.
  • The vertical edge \(AD\) of the sheared cube, \(\vek n = (0, 0, 1)\): the formula gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), but the exact strain is \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\). Here the whole shift of the end is transverse: \(\mat H\,\vek n = (0{,}001, 0, 0)\), so \(t = 0\) and \(p = 0{,}001\). The term we keep vanishes, and only the correction \(\tfrac12|\mat H\,\vek n|^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}001^2\) remains. After loading the edge is the hypotenuse with the vertical leg \(\ell\) and the horizontal leg \(s = 0{,}001\,\ell\), where \(\ell\) is the height of the cube:
    \[L_1 = \sqrt{\ell^2 + (0{,}001\,\ell)^2} = \ell\,\sqrt{1 + 10^{-6}} \approx \ell\,(1 + 5 \cdot 10^{-7}) .\]
    This is the vertical edge of section 1.6.2, which only tilts and whose strain grows with the square of the shift. The error \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) is small compared with the strains we care about, but it is not small compared with zero. The small strain tensor says that the edge does not get longer, while in fact it gets longer by a thousand times less than the diagonals.

Figure 1.397 shows \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) for all directions in one plane, on the left for the cube, on the right for the bar.

Let us draw the left graph, for the cube, directions in the plane \(x\)-\(z\). The axes show the component \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the direction and the strain \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\). The blue curve is \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\) for all such directions, from \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\) to \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\). The upper dot at \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 1/\sqrt2\) is the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) with the largest strain \(5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the lower dot at \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1/\sqrt2\) is the direction of the diagonal \(BD\) with the smallest, \(-5 \cdot 10^{-4}\). Grey dashed lines lead from each dot to the axis and to the value on the vertical axis. The right graph is for the bar, directions in the plane \(x\)-\(y\). The axes mean the same. The blue curve is \(\varepsilon = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\,(1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2)\). The upper dots at \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = \pm 1\) are the directions along the bar with the largest strain \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and a grey dashed rectangle leads to the value on the axis. The lower dot at \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) is the direction across the bar, with the strain \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\). The numbers \(\pm 0{,}48\) on the axis are the directions where the curve crosses the axis, that is, where the fibre does not change its length. The scales of the vertical axes differ, because the strains of the bar and of the cube are of very different sizes.

For the cube take the directions in the plane \(x\)-\(z\), \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, n_{\mathrm{z}})\), where \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = \sqrt{1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2}\). A fibre and the opposite fibre have the same strain, because in (1.53) all terms are products of two components of the direction, and these do not change when both change sign. So the directions with \(n_{\mathrm{z}} \ge 0\) are enough. By (1.53), \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0{,}001\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\). Why are the extreme values exactly in the directions of the diagonals? The square of the product is \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,(1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2) = \tfrac14 - \big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - \tfrac12\big)^2\), which is never larger than \(\tfrac14\) and equals \(\tfrac14\) exactly for \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = \tfrac12\). So \(|n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}| \le \tfrac12\), and the strain is largest, \(0{,}0005\), in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) and smallest, \(-0{,}0005\), in the direction of the diagonal \(BD\). The graph of the cube has at \(-n_{\mathrm{x}}\) the opposite value from that at \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\), because the product \(n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\) only changes into its negative. The direction with \(-n_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the mirror image of the direction with \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\) in the axis \(z\). A shear that lengthens one diagonal shortens the other, so it gives the mirror directions opposite strains. Near \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = \pm 1\) the graph is steep, because there \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = \sqrt{1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2}\) changes quickly: even a small turn of the direction away from the axis \(x\) gives a noticeable \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\). For the hanging bar at the point \(P\) take the directions in the plane \(x\)-\(y\), \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\). There \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\,(1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2)\): it is largest along the bar and smallest across it, and the fibres with \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| = 0{,}48\) do not change their length. We calculate this number in section 1.17.4.

What the individual numbers of the tensor \(\ten\varepsilon\) measure, we read from the formula (1.53). For a fibre along the axis \(x\), \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), only \(\varepsilon(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) remains, and the same for the axes \(y\) and \(z\): the entries \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are normal strains, the stretchings of fibres along the axes. For the diagonal fibre \(\vek n = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\) we have \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = \tfrac12\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) measures by how much the strain of the diagonal fibre differs from the average of the strains of the two fibres along the axes. This is the shear strain, and the same holds for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). For the cube \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005\) and the fibre in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) gets longer by exactly that much, while the fibres along the axes do not change. We explain this in detail in section 1.17.4.

1.17.4 What the components mean

The formula (1.53) keeps the promise of section 1.1. Let us write it once more, because we will use it all the time in this section:

\[\varepsilon(\vek n) \approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} .\]

The strain of a short fibre in every direction \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) through the point \(P\) is therefore determined by six numbers, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and we need nothing else for it (SADD §2.2, PDF p. 43). The factor \(2\) in front of the last three terms is there because the double sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) has each such term twice, once above the diagonal of the matrix and once below it: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\) are equal, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). What does each of the six numbers measure?

The figure shows the table of the numbers \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) in the rows and columns \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The grey cells on the diagonal have equal indices. The blue cells above the diagonal have different indices, and the blue cells below it are their mirror image with the same numbers, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Every symmetric matrix has such a pattern, and the table shows only which places are equal.

Let us start with the numbers with equal indices. For a fibre along the axis \(x\), with \(\vek n = (1, 0, 0)\), only the first term remains in (1.53), \(\varepsilon(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) \approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). So the number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the relative change of length of a short fibre along the axis \(x\), the normal strain in the direction of the axis \(x\) (definition 1.3). In the same way \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are the normal strains in the directions of the axes \(y\) and \(z\). When there are no shear strains, a small cube of material with edge \(h\) and edges along the axes becomes a box with the edges \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\,h\), \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\,h\) and \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,h\) (figure 1.399).

The axes on the left show \(x\) to the right, \(y\) back into the depth and \(z\) upwards. The blackwhite cube is a small piece of material before loading, the grey dashed edges are those that the body hides. Each edge is \(h\) long: the one at the front in the direction of the axis \(x\), the one at the side in the direction of the axis \(y\) and the one at the left edge in the direction of the axis \(z\). The point \(P\) is the bottom front left corner. The orange box is the same piece after loading, when only the normal strains are different from zero, its hidden edges are again grey dashed. The right angles stay right angles, because there are no shear strains. The edge along the axis \(x\) is \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\,h\) long, the edge along the axis \(y\) is \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\,h\) long and the edge along the axis \(z\) is \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,h\) long. In the figure \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is negative, so the edge along the axis \(y\) is shorter than \(h\). The strains are greatly magnified so that the differences can be seen.

Let us test this on the hanging bar, which hangs under its own weight, with the axis \(x\) pointing down from the centre \(O\) of the top end. A point on the axis of the bar moves down by \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), where \(L = 10\) m is the length of the bar and \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}^{-1}\) is a number that, by section 1.2, depends only on how heavy the steel is and how strongly it resists stretching. The unit \(\mathrm{m}^{-1}\) is such that \(a\) times the square of a length is again a length. We differentiate with respect to \(x\):

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} = a\,(2L - 2x) = 2a\,(L - x) .\]

This is the strain at a point from definition 1.10, which we defined for the bar in section 1.4. So the strain at a point of the bar is the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of the small strain tensor. It is largest at the top, at \(x = 0\), where the pull is largest, and zero at the bottom end, at \(x = L\), as we saw in section 1.2. At the point \(P\) of the bar, which is \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m below \(O\), we have

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2a\,(L - x_{\mathrm{P}}) = 2 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}^{-1} \cdot 5\ \mathrm{m} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} .\]

And the numbers with different indices? The answer comes from a fibre along the diagonal of a small square. Let us first draw the square and both diagonal fibres from the point \(P\) (figure 1.400).

The axes at the bottom left show \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards. The point \(P\) is the corner of the square, and the blackwhite square is a small piece of material before loading, drawn relative to \(P\). Its edges are \(h\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) and \(h\) in the direction of the axis \(y\) long. The small grey angle at \(P\) is the right angle between them. The orange rhombus is the same piece after loading, when only the shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is different from zero. In the figure both partial derivatives of which \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is made are equal, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and the other two derivatives in the plane are zero. When the derivatives are not equal, the piece in addition turns as a whole, which we look at in section 1.17.5. By lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading, the end of the edge along the axis \(x\) moves by \(h\) times the first column of the matrix \(\mat H\), and the end of the edge along the axis \(y\) by \(h\) times the second column:

\[h\begin{bmatrix} \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x \\ \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,h \end{bmatrix} , \qquad h\begin{bmatrix} \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y \\ \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,h \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The grey dimensions show these shifts: the end of the edge along the axis \(x\) goes up by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,h\), the end of the edge along the axis \(y\) to the right by the same distance. So the edges tilt towards each other, and the orange angle at \(P\) is smaller than a right angle. The lengths of the edges change only by terms with the square of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so almost not at all.

The fibre from \(P\) along the first diagonal is grey before loading, orange after it, and longer. Both lie on the same line, so the grey one is drawn wider under the orange one and is seen as an edge beside it. The fibre from \(P\) in the direction of the second diagonal points up and to the left, out of the square into the material on the other side of the point \(P\), which we do not draw. The grey dot is its end before loading, the orange one after it. The end moves along the fibre towards \(P\), so the fibre stays on the same line and gets shorter. The second diagonal of the square, grey dashed before loading and orange after it, is parallel to this fibre. It gets shorter by the same fraction, because to first order the displacement gradient is the same at all points near \(P\), and parallel fibres therefore change in the same way. The deformation is greatly magnified so that the differences can be seen.

Let us compute the strains of both fibres with the formula. The fibre along the first diagonal has the direction \(\vek n = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\), so \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = n_{\mathrm{y}} = 1/\sqrt2\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). Therefore \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = \tfrac12\), and all terms with \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero. We substitute:

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon\big((1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\big) &\approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} \cdot \tfrac12 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} \cdot \tfrac12 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} \cdot 0 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot \tfrac12 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} \cdot 0 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} \cdot 0 \\ &= \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} . \end{aligned}\]

The fibre in the direction of the second diagonal, \(\vek n = (-1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\), also has \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = \tfrac12\), only the product \(n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = -\tfrac12\) has the opposite sign:

\[\varepsilon\big((-1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\big) \approx \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot \big(-\tfrac12\big) = \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]

The fibres along the axes \(x\) and \(y\) have the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and their average is \(\tfrac12(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\). Let us subtract it from the strains of both diagonal fibres:

\[\varepsilon\big((1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\big) - \tfrac12\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\big) \approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} , \qquad \varepsilon\big((-1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\big) - \tfrac12\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\big) \approx -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]

So the number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) tells by how much the first diagonal stretches more than the average of the fibres along the axes \(x\) and \(y\), and the second by as much less. The difference between the two diagonals is \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). When \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the only nonzero component, the fibres along the axes do not get longer, one diagonal gets longer and the other shorter. The same happened with the deck of cards of section 1.1: when we pushed it sideways at the top, the diagonal from the bottom left to the top right corner got longer and the other one shorter. The deck also turns in the process, as we will see for the sheared cube in section 1.17.5, but a turn does not change lengths.

We see the same number also in the tilt of the fibres. First let us write down what \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is made of, by definition 1.115:

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) .\]

What the two partial derivatives in the brackets mean, we draw on two short fibres from the point \(P\) (figure 1.401).

Let us draw the left half. The point \(P\) is the common start of both fibres. The blackwhite fibres from \(P\) lie along the axes, the horizontal fibre along the axis \(x\) and the vertical one along the axis \(y\), both of length \(h\). The orange fibres are the same fibres after loading. By lemma 1.111 the end of the fibre along the axis \(x\) moves by \(h\) times the first column of the matrix \(\mat H\), which is \(\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x,\ \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x,\ \partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x\big)\). Its sideways shift, in the direction of the axis \(y\), is the second component, \(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\,h\), which the grey scale beside it shows. The end of the fibre along the axis \(y\) moves by \(h\) times the second column, and its sideways shift, in the direction of the axis \(x\), is the first component, \(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\,h\), which the grey scale above it shows. In the figure \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) are zero, so the ends move only sideways, and the lengths of the fibres change only by terms with squares. The ratios of the sideways shift of the end to the length of the fibre are therefore \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\), numbers without a unit, and by the definition of the number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) their sum is

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]

Both ratios are positive in the figure, so the fibres tilt towards each other. The grey arc is the angle between them after loading, which is smaller than a right angle.

By how much does the right angle decrease? The blue arc \(\theta_1\) is the angle by which the fibre along the axis \(x\) turns towards the axis \(y\), and the blue arc \(\theta_2\) is the angle by which the fibre along the axis \(y\) turns towards the axis \(x\). We measure angles in radians, by the length of an arc on a circle of radius \(1\) (definition 1.3), so the right angle is a quarter of the circumference \(2\pi\), that is, \(\pi/2\). In the figure the right angle between the axes is made of three pieces: \(\theta_1\), the angle between the orange fibres and \(\theta_2\). The angle between the fibres after loading is therefore exactly \(\pi/2 - \theta_1 - \theta_2\). The right angle decreases by the sum \(\theta_1 + \theta_2\), not by the difference, because each fibre turns towards the other. The orange fibre along the axis \(x\) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the legs \(h\) and \(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\,h\), so the tangent of the angle \(\theta_1\) equals \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\). For a small angle, the angle in radians is almost equal to its tangent (section 1.6.2). The same holds for \(\theta_2\). Let us write it on the board:

\[\frac{\pi}{2} - (\text{angle between the fibres after loading}) = \theta_1 + \theta_2 \approx \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]

How accurate is the sign \(\approx\)? For the sheared cube the tangent of the angle by which the vertical edge tilts is exactly \(s/h = 0{,}001\), while the angle itself is \(0{,}00099999967\) rad, which we compute with a computer. They differ by \(3{,}3 \cdot 10^{-10}\), by three ten-millionths of the angle. When the fibre along the axis \(x\) also gets longer, the horizontal leg is \((1 + \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x)\,h\), and the tangent of the angle \(\theta_1\) is \(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} \big/ \big(1 + \tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}\big)\). It differs from \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) by a term with the product of two partial derivatives. The right angle between the positive directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) therefore decreases by \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), expressed in radians, that is, as the length of an arc on a circle of radius \(1\), accurate up to terms with products of partial derivatives.

The right half is drawn in the same way, with the point \(P\), the blackwhite fibres along the axis \(x\) and the axis \(y\), and the orange ones after loading. The shift beside the fibre along the axis \(x\) is again upwards and the same as before. The shift beside the fibre along the axis \(y\) is now to the left. The dimension is \(-\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\,h\) long, because \(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\) is negative here. The ratios are equal and of opposite signs, so the fibres turn in the same sense. The grey right-angle mark says that the angle between them stays a right angle.

When both ratios are positive, the fibres tilt towards each other, and the right angle between the positive directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) decreases by their sum. But when the ratios are equal and of opposite signs, the sum is zero. Then the fibres tilt in the same sense of turning, and the right angle stays a right angle. This is so for the hanging bar of section 1.7.2, where \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = -\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\), so there both fibres turned in the same direction. The shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) therefore measures the part of the tilting that changes the right angle. We will derive the exact relation between \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the decrease of the right angle, which also holds for large partial derivatives, in chapter 2, when we know how to measure angles between arbitrary vectors (CM (3.5.9), PDF p. 142, SADD (2.2.3), PDF p. 43). SADD fixes the sign in the same way: the shear strain is positive when the right angle between the positive directions of the axes decreases (SADD, PDF p. 43).

Let us test both on the sheared cube, which is glued to the table by its bottom face and whose top face moves by \(s = 10\) µm at the height \(h = 10\,000\) µm. The axis \(x\) points in the direction of the shift, the axis \(z\) upwards. The displacement field is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = (s/h)\,z = 0{,}001\,z\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) ((1.16)). The only nonzero partial derivative is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z = 0{,}001\), so by definition 1.115

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(0{,}001 + 0) = 0{,}0005 = \frac{s}{2h} ,\]

and the other components are zero. For example \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = 0\), because \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) does not depend on \(x\). The vertical edge \(AD\) tilts in the direction of the axis \(x\) by the ratio \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z = 0{,}001 = s/h\), while the bottom edge \(AB\) does not tilt, because \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x = 0\). The sum of the ratios is \(0{,}001 = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), and by that much, measured as the length of an arc on a circle of radius \(1\), about \(0{,}057^\circ\), the right angle at the corner \(A\) decreases. The diagonal \(AC\) has the direction \(\vek n = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\) with \(n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac12\), and the diagonal \(BD\) the direction \(\vek n = (-1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\) with \(n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = -\tfrac12\). Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are zero, only the term \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\) remains in the formula:

\[\varepsilon(AC) \approx 2 \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot \tfrac12 = 0{,}0005 , \qquad \varepsilon(BD) \approx 2 \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot \big(-\tfrac12\big) = -0{,}0005 .\]

Now we see where the half came from in section 1.6.2, where the diagonals changed by half the ratio \(s/h\). The tilt \(s/h\) of the edge is the sum of both ratios, \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), while a diagonal stretches only by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\).

This half is a source of frequent mistakes. Many books and programs for structural calculations use, instead of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the sum of both ratios, the engineering shear strain (inženirska strižna deformacija)

\[\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} ,\]

and likewise \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) (SADD (2.2.4), PDF p. 43, CM, PDF p. 141). BOWER warns that this factor of \(2\) is an endless source of confusion, and advises us to check, for every shear strain reported, which of the two is meant (BOWER §2.1.8, PDF p. 51). In this book a shear strain will always be \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), because with it the formula (1.53) is a plain double sum with a symmetric matrix. Let us write the formula with both notations, one below the other:

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon(\vek n) &\approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} \\ &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned}\]

The first row is the double sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) with the matrix \(\ten\varepsilon\). The second has the mixed terms without the factor \(2\), but a matrix with the entries \(\gamma\) cannot be put into a double sum, because off the diagonal we would have to write \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}/2\). For the cube \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}001\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005\).

Let us return to the hanging bar, which hangs under its own weight, with the axis \(x\) pointing down from the centre \(O\) of the top end. Its displacement field (1.18) is

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

where \(0{,}3\) is the Poisson ratio of steel, the ratio of thinning to stretching from section 1.6. Let us write the table of partial derivatives from section 1.7.2 once more. The row tells which component of the displacement we differentiate, the column with respect to which coordinate:

\(\partial / \partial x\) \(\partial / \partial y\) \(\partial / \partial z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(2a\,(L - x)\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) \(0\)
\(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) \(0{,}6\,a\,z\) \(0\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\)

By definition 1.115 we take on the diagonal of the table the derivatives themselves, and off it half the sum of the derivative above the diagonal and the derivative below it. At every point of the bar we therefore have

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 2a\,(L - x) , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0 , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,z + 0{,}6\,a\,z) = 0 , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \tfrac12\,(0 + 0) = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

There are no shear strains anywhere in the bar, as we predicted in words in section 1.7.2 and as CM also finds (CM Example 7.3.2, equation (3), PDF p. 305). The pairs of equal and opposite partial derivatives cancel in the sum. The transverse normal strains are \(-0{,}3\) times the axial one, \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = -0{,}3 \cdot 2a\,(L - x)\), which is the thinning of section 1.6.

Now we also understand the fibre in the direction \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\), which got shorter. In the formula (1.53) the three shear terms are zero, and in the other two we factor out \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}3 \cdot 2a\,(L - x)\):

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon(\vek n) &\approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 0 + 0 + 0 \\ &= 2a\,(L - x)\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}3 \cdot 2a\,(L - x)\,\big(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\big) \\ &= 2a\,(L - x)\,\big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}3\,(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\big) = 2a\,(L - x)\,\big(\tfrac19 - 0{,}3 \cdot \tfrac89\big) . \end{aligned}\]

In figure 1.390 the axis \(x\) points down, and \(\varepsilon\) means the axial strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2a\,(L - x)\) at the point \(P\). The part of the fibre along the bar has length \(\tfrac13\,h\) and stretches by the factor \(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The transverse part of the fibre has the direction \((0, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\) and length

\[\sqrt{\big(\tfrac23\big)^2 + \big(\tfrac23\big)^2}\;h = \sqrt{\tfrac89}\;h = \frac{\sqrt8}{3}\,h ,\]

and shrinks by the factor \(1 - 0{,}3\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The fibre therefore lies mostly across the bar, \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = \tfrac89\), and across the bar the bar gets thinner. Let us write the two terms in the brackets one below the other:

part term value
stretching along the bar \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) \(\tfrac19 = 0{,}111\)
thinning across the bar \(-0{,}3\,(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\) \(-0{,}3 \cdot \tfrac89 = -0{,}267\)
total \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}3\,(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\) \(-0{,}156\)

The thinning across the bar wins over the stretching along it, so the fibre gets shorter, although its end moves down more than \(P\). At the point \(P\) we have, as we calculated at the beginning of the section, \(2a\,(L - x_{\mathrm{P}}) = 2 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}^{-1} \cdot 5\ \mathrm{m} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and

\[\varepsilon(\vek n) \approx 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot (-0{,}155556) = -3{,}0364 \cdot 10^{-7} ,\]

which is the value from section 1.17.3.

Which fibres through \(P\) keep their length? The vector \(\vek n\) is a unit vector, so \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = 1\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = 1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2\). The strain of the fibre therefore depends on only one component of the direction, \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\):

\[\varepsilon(\vek n) \approx 2a\,(L - x)\,\big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}3\,(1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2)\big) = 2a\,(L - x)\,\big(1{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}3\big) .\]

It is zero at \(1{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 0{,}3\), that is, at \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 0{,}3/1{,}3 = 0{,}2308\) and \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| = 0{,}48\). Such fibres do not change their length. These are the zeros of the graph on the right side of figure 1.397, which therefore draws the strain against \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\) alone.

The normal strains also tell how the volume of a small piece changes. With normal strains alone, a small cube with edge \(h\) becomes a box with the volume

\[\begin{aligned} (1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,h^3 &= \big(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} \\ &\quad + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\big)\,h^3 . \end{aligned}\]

We leave out products of two or three strains for small deformations: for strains of about \(0{,}001\) a product of two is about \(10^{-6}\), a thousand times less than the sum of the first three terms.

And the shear strains? Let us draw two examples in the plane, the area of a face before loading and after it (figure 1.402).

On the left is the front face of the sheared cube before loading, a blackwhite square with the corners \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\). The orange parallelogram is the same face after loading, the corners \(C\) and \(D\) move to \(C_1\) and \(D_1\). The top edge moves by \(s\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), while the bottom edge \(AB\) stays on the table, so the square and the parallelogram have the same base. The height \(h\) does not change, because \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and the top edge stays at the same height. The area of a parallelogram is base times height, so it equals the area of the square, \(h^2\). The shift \(s\) is greatly magnified.

On the right is a square with the corner \(P\) and the side \(h\), which the shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) turns without a turn of the piece into a rhombus, the same as above. The diagonal \(d_1\) is the fibre along the first diagonal, lengthened by the factor \(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and the diagonal \(d_2\) is the fibre along the second diagonal, shortened by the factor \(1 - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\):

\[d_1 = \sqrt2\,h\,(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}) , \qquad d_2 = \sqrt2\,h\,(1 - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}) .\]

We saw that both diagonal fibres stay on their lines, so the diagonals stay perpendicular. They cut the rhombus into four right triangles with the legs \(d_1/2\) and \(d_2/2\), so its area is

\[4 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \frac{d_1}{2} \cdot \frac{d_2}{2} = \frac{d_1\,d_2}{2} = \frac{\sqrt2\,h\,(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}) \cdot \sqrt2\,h\,(1 - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}})}{2} = h^2\,\big(1 - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\big) .\]

The area changes only by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\,h^2\), for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}001\) by a millionth. In both examples shear does not change the area to first order.

The same holds in space: shear strains change only the right angles and for small deformations do not change the volume (BOWER §2.1.9, PDF p. 52). The general case, in which shear and normal strains in all three planes mix, we do not prove here, since it needs a calculation with three vectors at once. The proof is in section 2.10.5 of chapter 2, in item 2 of lemma 2.55: the volume of a piece is multiplied by the number \(\det\mat F\), which is a sum of products of three entries of the matrix \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\), and for small partial derivatives only \(1\) and the three diagonal entries of first degree remain of these products, which give the trace. There we also get the exact relation, which also holds for large deformations. So the fraction by which the volume of a small piece changes is about

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \tr\ten\varepsilon ,\]

the sum of the diagonal entries of the matrix, which we call the trace (sled) of the matrix (BOWER §2.1.9, PDF p. 51, SADD §2.4, PDF p. 49). For the sheared cube the trace is zero, which agrees with the finding of section 1.6.2 that simple shear does not change the volume. For the hanging bar at the point \(P\) the trace is

\[1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - 2 \cdot 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7} ,\]

which is \((1 - 2 \cdot 0{,}3)\) times, that is \(0{,}4\) times, the axial strain. The volume grows because the bar gets thinner across by less than it gets longer. For an axial strain of \(0{,}001\) the relative change would be \(0{,}0004\), which in section 1.6 we got from \(1{,}001 \cdot 0{,}9997^2 \approx 1{,}0004\).

The graph in figure 1.397 shows one more thing. For the cube the strain is largest in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) and smallest in the direction of the diagonal \(BD\), for the bar largest along the bar and smallest across it. Books show that for every small deformation there are three mutually perpendicular directions in which there is no shear, only stretching or compression, and that among all fibres through the point the largest and the smallest strain occur in these directions (SADD §2.4, PDF pp. 48-49, and §1.6, PDF p. 22). A direction without shear means: the right angle between a fibre in this direction and a fibre in any direction perpendicular to it stays a right angle to first order. We already announced this in section 1.1. For the hanging bar these are the directions of the axes, because all three shear strains are zero and no right angle between the axes changes. For the cube it is the direction of the axis \(y\), because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero. The other two are the directions of the two diagonals of the front face. Shear in a plane leaves the diagonals of the rhombus perpendicular, as we saw above, and the face of the cube in addition turns as a whole, which turns both diagonals equally. The proof that such three directions exist for every deformation needs calculations with angles between arbitrary vectors, so we will do it in chapter 2, together with stresses (section 2.11.4). Why are we interested in these directions? In them the material is stretched the most and the least.

Let us collect what the components of the small strain tensor mean:

quantity meaning figure
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) relative change of length of a short fibre along the axis the cube becomes a box
\(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) decrease of the right angle between the positive directions of the axes, in radians the fibres tilt towards each other
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) by how much a diagonal stretches more than the average of the fibres along the axes the longer and the shorter diagonal
\(\tr\ten\varepsilon\) relative change of volume of a small piece the box and the rhombus

Each meaning holds to first order, accurate up to terms with products of partial derivatives. We will need the separation into the change of lengths and the change of angles for stresses, where a normal strain corresponds to the part of the force perpendicular to a surface and a shear strain to the part of the force in the surface (definition 1.3).

1.17.5 The turning of the material near a point

The small strain tensor is the symmetric part of the matrix \(\mat H\). By lemma 1.103 on the split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts, \(\mat H\) is the sum of its symmetric and antisymmetric parts, and this split is unique. What does the antisymmetric part describe? We will show that it is a turn of the material near the point: the part of the motion in which the distances between nearby points do not change, and which is therefore not a deformation.

Definition 1.116 Small rotation tensor (tenzor malih zasukov)

Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient at an interior point \(P\) of a body. The small rotation tensor at the point \(P\) (tenzor malih zasukov) is the matrix

\[\ten\omega = \tfrac12\big(\mat H - \mat H^\T\big) , \tag{1.54}\]

with the entries \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} - H_{\mathrm{ji}})\), written out

\[\ten\omega = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \omega_{\mathrm{xy}} & \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ -\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} & 0 & \omega_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ -\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} & -\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

where \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y - \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\big)\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z - \partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x\big)\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z - \partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial y\big)\), all at the point \(P\).

Source: CM (3.5.10), (3.5.11) (PDF p. 143), where the symbol is \(\boldsymbol\Omega\), SADD (2.1.7) (PDF p. 40), BOWER §2.1.10 (PDF p. 52).

Why the name turn, and why exactly this order of the derivatives? Take a small turn of a body as a whole about the axis \(z\) by the angle \(\theta\) in radians from section 1.6, positive from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\). The displacement of the point \((x, y, z)\) is there \(\vek u \approx (-\theta\,y,\ \theta\,x,\ 0)\), so \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = -\theta\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = \theta\), and the derivatives of these derivatives, for example the derivative of \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) with respect to \(x\), are zero. By definition

\[\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(-\theta - \theta) = -\theta , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(-\theta + \theta) = 0 .\]

The entry \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is therefore the angle of the turn about the axis \(z\) in radians, with the opposite sign. A positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) turns from the axis \(y\) towards the axis \(x\), which is a clockwise turn when we look from the end of the axis \(z\). The small strain tensor of this displacement is the zero matrix, as it must be, because the body does not deform. We calculate the other two turns in the same way. For a small turn about the axis \(y\) by the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{y}}\), from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(x\), the displacement is \(\vek u \approx (\theta_{\mathrm{y}}\,z,\ 0,\ -\theta_{\mathrm{y}}\,x)\), and for a turn about the axis \(x\) by the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{x}}\), from the axis \(y\) towards the axis \(z\), it is \(\vek u \approx (0,\ -\theta_{\mathrm{x}}\,z,\ \theta_{\mathrm{x}}\,y)\). From the definition it follows that

\[\begin{aligned} \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(\theta_{\mathrm{y}} + \theta_{\mathrm{y}}) = \theta_{\mathrm{y}} , \\ \omega_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(-\theta_{\mathrm{x}} - \theta_{\mathrm{x}}) = -\theta_{\mathrm{x}} , \end{aligned}\]

in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) we have \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\theta\). In all three cases \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the angle of the turn from the axis \(\ix{j}\) towards the axis \(\ix{i}\): \(-\theta\) for \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\theta_{\mathrm{y}}\) for \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(-\theta_{\mathrm{x}}\) for \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\). We remember the rule for all three entries like this: a positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) turns from the axis \(\ix{j}\) towards the axis \(\ix{i}\), about the third axis, by the angle \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) in radians (figure 1.403).

In each panel of the figure the axis of the first index points to the right and the axis of the second upwards. On the left are the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The circle with a dot at the origin is the axis \(z\), which points towards the reader, because by the right-hand rule the fingers point from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\) and the thumb along the axis \(z\) (a right-handed system). The blue arc shows the direction of turning for a positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\): from the axis \(y\) towards the axis \(x\). In the middle are the axes \(x\) and \(z\). The third axis, \(y\), points away from the reader here, which the circle with a cross tells. The arc shows that a positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) turns from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(x\). On the right are the axes \(y\) and \(z\), the axis \(x\) points towards the reader, and the arc shows that a positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\) turns from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(y\). In all three panels a positive entry turns clockwise, because we always draw the axis of the first index to the right. How the turns in the three planes combine into a single turn about one axis, we do not need here. For that we would need a calculation that gives from two vectors a third, perpendicular to both, and we meet this calculation in chapter 2.

On the diagonal there are zeros, because \(\omega_{\mathrm{ii}} = \tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ii}} - H_{\mathrm{ii}}) = 0\), and below the diagonal the opposite values of those above it, because \(\omega_{\mathrm{ji}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\). So the matrix has only three different numbers. We have \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\), which we check entry by entry: \(\tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}}) + \tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} - H_{\mathrm{ji}}) = H_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading, the difference of the displacements of the ends of a short fibre is, up to the remainders, \(\mat H\,(h\,\vek n)\), so

\[\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P) \approx h\,\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + h\,\ten\omega\,\vek n . \tag{1.55}\]

We already know the first part: it gives the strain of the fibre. What does the second part do? Figure 1.404 shows both parts on a small square: the change by the matrix \(\mat H\) is the sum of the change by the symmetric part and the turn by the antisymmetric part. Let us show that the second part changes the length of no fibre, up to terms with squares of partial derivatives.

Let us draw the left half. The axes at the bottom left show \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards. The point \(P\) is the corner of a small square. The blackwhite square is the square before loading, the orange quadrilateral is the one after the change by \(\mat H\), the label below it says by which matrix. The shifts of the ends of the edges are the grey dimension at the edge along the axis \(x\) and the grey dimension at the edge along the axis \(y\). The sign \(=\) says that this change equals the sum of the changes in the middle and on the right.

In the middle is the symmetric part. It is drawn in the same way: the square, the orange quadrilateral after this part and the grey dimensions of the shifts of the ends of the edges, along the axis \(x\) and along the axis \(y\). Below it is the label \(\ten\varepsilon\). The edges get longer or shorter and tilt towards each other. The sign \(+\) adds the antisymmetric part on the right, with the same square, the orange quadrilateral, the grey dimensions of the shifts of the ends, along the axis \(x\) and along the axis \(y\), and the label \(\ten\omega\). Here the square only turns, because both edges tilt equally in the same sense of turning. The shifts of the ends of the edges on the left are the sums of the shifts in the middle and on the right. The point \(P\) is drawn in the same place in all three (middle, right).

In the figure the numbers are greatly magnified so that the shifts can be seen. The left, middle and right change are drawn with the matrices

\[\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0{,}20 & -0{,}08 \\ 0{,}32 & -0{,}10 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mat{H}} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0{,}20 & 0{,}12 \\ 0{,}12 & -0{,}10 \end{bmatrix}}_{\ten{\varepsilon}} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -0{,}20 \\ 0{,}20 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\ten{\omega}} .\]

The entry in the row \(x\) and column \(y\) we get from the entries \(H_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}08\) and \(H_{\mathrm{yx}} = 0{,}32\):

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(-0{,}08 + 0{,}32) = 0{,}12 , \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(-0{,}08 - 0{,}32) = -0{,}20 .\]

The entry \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is negative here. The right panel shows what this means: the columns of the matrix \(\ten\omega\) are \((0,\ 0{,}20)\) and \((-0{,}20,\ 0)\), so the end of the edge along the axis \(x\) moves up, by \(0{,}20\,h\), and the end of the edge along the axis \(y\) to the left, by \(0{,}20\,h\). The square therefore turns from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\). On the diagonal \(\ten\varepsilon\) has the diagonal of the matrix \(\mat H\), and \(\ten\omega\) has two zeros. The shift of the end of the edge along the axis \(x\) on the left is \(h\) times the first column of the matrix \(\mat H\), \((0{,}20,\ 0{,}32)\,h\), and it is the sum of the shift in the middle, \((0{,}20,\ 0{,}12)\,h\), and the shift on the right, \((0,\ 0{,}20)\,h\).

Let us draw why a turn does not change the length, in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane. The axes at the bottom left show \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards. The point \(P\) is the start of the fibre, the blackwhite arrow is the unit vector \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}})\), in the figure \((0{,}766,\ 0{,}643)\). In the plane \(\ten\omega\) has a single entry \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -a\), and we multiply the matrix by the vector row by row:

\[\ten\omega\,\vek n = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a \\ a & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} n_{\mathrm{x}} \\ n_{\mathrm{y}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -a\,n_{\mathrm{y}} \\ a\,n_{\mathrm{x}} \end{bmatrix} = a\begin{bmatrix} -n_{\mathrm{y}} \\ n_{\mathrm{x}} \end{bmatrix} .\]

This is the vector \(\vek n\) turned by a right angle towards the axis \(y\) and multiplied by \(a\). In the figure \(a = 0{,}3\), greatly magnified, so \(\ten\omega\,\vek n = (-0{,}193,\ 0{,}230)\). It is drawn from the end of the vector \(\vek n\) sideways, in blue, with a right angle between the two. The orange arrow is the vector \(\vek n + \ten\omega\,\vek n\), the fibre after the turn. We calculate the square of its length by components:

\[(n_{\mathrm{x}} - a\,n_{\mathrm{y}})^2 + (n_{\mathrm{y}} + a\,n_{\mathrm{x}})^2 = (1 + a^2)\,(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2) = 1 + a^2 ,\]

because the mixed terms \(-2a\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(2a\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\) cancel. In the figure the length is \(\sqrt{1{,}09} = 1{,}044\), so the end lies almost on the circle of radius \(1\): it is above it only by about \(\tfrac12\,a^2 = 0{,}045\), which is the quadratic term that we leave out in the first approximation. So the length of the fibre does not change, the fibre only turns. How the computation shows this for an arbitrary \(\ten\omega\) in space, we see in the steps below. The goal: in the first-order change of the square of the length of the fibre only \(\ten\varepsilon\) remains.

  1. Without the remainders the fibre after loading has the vector \(h\,(\vek n + \mat H\,\vek n)\). We write the square of its length component by component as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre:
    \[h^2\,|\vek n + \mat H\,\vek n|^2 = h^2\Big(|\vek n|^2 + 2\sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\mat H\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{i}} + |\mat H\,\vek n|^2\Big) .\]
  2. The first term is \(h^2\,|\vek n|^2 = h^2\), the square of the length before loading, because \(\vek n\) is a unit vector. The last is the square of a small number. So the first-order change is the middle term, and in it \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\mat H\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek n^\T\mat H\,\vek n\).
  3. Since \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\), we have \(\vek n^\T\mat H\,\vek n = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + \vek n^\T\ten\omega\,\vek n\).
  4. In the double sum \(\vek n^\T\ten\omega\,\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) the terms with \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) are zero, because \(\omega_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\). Every term with \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\) has a partner in the sum with the indices swapped, and \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} + n_{\mathrm{j}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ji}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\,(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ji}}) = 0\). There are three such pairs:
    \[\vek n^\T\ten\omega\,\vek n = n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\,(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} + \omega_{\mathrm{yx}}) + n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\,(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} + \omega_{\mathrm{zx}}) + n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\,(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} + \omega_{\mathrm{zy}}) = 0 + 0 + 0 .\]
    So \(\vek n^\T\ten\omega\,\vek n = 0\), which in the plane means that \(\ten\omega\,\vek n\) is perpendicular to \(\vek n\).
  5. The first-order change of the square of the length is therefore \(2h^2\,\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), and the matrix \(\ten\omega\) does not appear in it. We divide it by \(2L_0^2 = 2h^2\) and get the strain of the fibre from section 1.17.3:
    \[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_0^2} \approx \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n \approx \varepsilon(\vek n) .\]

So the part \(h\,\ten\omega\,\vek n\) moves the end of the fibre in such a way that the length of the fibre does not change to first order: the fibre only turns. This holds for all directions at once, with the same matrix \(\ten\omega\), and more follows from it: the distances between other points near \(P\) do not change either (figure 1.406).

The axes at the bottom left show \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards. The point \(P\) is the point about which we observe the material. The point \(Q\) and the point \(Q'\) are two points near \(P\), and the blackwhite arrow is the vector \(\overrightarrow{QQ'}\) between them. The grey dashed segments join both points with \(P\). The blue arrow at \(Q\) is the part of the displacement of the point \(Q\) relative to \(P\) that \(\ten\omega\) gives, that is \(\ten\omega\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\), and the blue arrow at \(Q'\) is \(\ten\omega\,\overrightarrow{PQ'}\). Each is perpendicular to its grey segment and the longer, the farther the point is from \(P\), as for a turn about \(P\). In the figure \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}3\), greatly magnified. The orange points \(Q_1\) and \(Q_1'\) are the new positions, and the orange segment between them is the distance after the displacement.

The blue arrows differ by \(\ten\omega\) times the vector \(\overrightarrow{QQ'}\), because \(\ten\omega\,\overrightarrow{PQ'} - \ten\omega\,\overrightarrow{PQ} = \ten\omega\,\big(\overrightarrow{PQ'} - \overrightarrow{PQ}\big)\) (lemma 1.97 and item 3 of lemma 1.99). Steps 1 to 4, however, do not require a unit vector, if we write \(|\vek v|^2\) instead of \(h^2\) (for a vector \(\vek v\) the first term is \(|\vek v|^2\) and the change is still \(2\,\vek v^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek v\)), so they hold for every vector, also for \(\overrightarrow{QQ'}\). The orange segment is therefore, to first order, as long as the blackwhite arrow. In the figure they are \(1{,}995\) and \(1{,}910\) long, the ratio is \(\sqrt{1 + 0{,}3^2} = 1{,}044\), and the difference is again a quadratic term. To first order, therefore, no distance between points near \(P\) changes, and the material near \(P\) moves as a rigid body (definition 1.11). All short fibres through \(P\) thus turn together. CM shows that a displacement given by an antisymmetric matrix that is the same at all points is a rigid turn when its entries are small (CM, PDF p. 143). Hence the name small rotation tensor. To first order, the material close to the point deforms according to \(\ten\varepsilon\) and at the same time turns according to \(\ten\omega\) (figure 1.404). SADD (2.1.8) (PDF p. 40) and BOWER (PDF p. 52) split the change in the same way.

Let us check the direction of turning, which we got at the definition from the turn about the axis \(z\), also with the columns of the matrix \(\ten\omega\). The part \(h\,\ten\omega\,\vek n\) moves the end of the fibre, and for a fibre along the axis \(\ix{j}\) this is \(h\) times the column \(\ix{j}\) of the matrix \(\ten\omega\). For a fibre along the axis \(y\) the second column is \((\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}, 0, -\omega_{\mathrm{yz}})\): the end moves in the direction of the axis \(x\) by \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\,h\). For a fibre along the axis \(x\) the first column is \((0, -\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}, -\omega_{\mathrm{xz}})\): the end moves in the direction of the axis \(y\) by \(-\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\,h\). A positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) therefore turns the material in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) from the axis \(y\) towards the axis \(x\), and a negative one from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\). In the same way a positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) turns in the plane \(x\)-\(z\) from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(x\), and a positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\) in the plane \(y\)-\(z\) from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(y\). The size of an entry is the ratio of the sideways shift of the end to the length of the fibre. For a small angle this ratio is almost equal to the angle in radians, as we saw for the tilt of the fibres in section 1.17.4, so \(|\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}|\) is the angle of the turn in radians.

For the hanging bar we take the derivatives from the table in section 1.17.4 at the point \(P\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 0{,}004\) m and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\):

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} = -0{,}6\,a\,y_{\mathrm{P}} = -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = 0{,}6\,a\,y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} .\]

So

\[\begin{aligned} \omega_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \tfrac12\big(-4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} - 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\big) = -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} , \\ \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,z_{\mathrm{P}} - 0{,}6\,a\,z_{\mathrm{P}}) = 0 , \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12\,(0 - 0) = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

The first minus in the brackets is the sign of the derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\), the second is the minus from the definition in front of the positive derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\). Since at the same time \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), the material near \(P\) only turns in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) and is not sheared. The entry \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is negative, so the material turns from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\), by the angle \(4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\) rad: a fibre along the axis \(x\) tilts towards the positive axis \(y\), and a fibre along the axis \(y\) towards the negative axis \(x\). We described this in words in section 1.7.2. In figure 1.100 the axis of the bar runs vertically, the axis \(x\) along it downwards, which the arrow to the left of the bar shows, and the axis \(y\) to the right. The orange fibres are the fibres along the axis \(x\) after loading: the lower end of each is shifted to the right relative to the upper one, in the direction of the axis \(y\). The orange cross-section, a fibre along the axis \(y\), rises towards the edge, that is, moves in the direction \(-x\). Both are the same turn of the material, so the right angles between them stay right angles. The tilt is extremely magnified in the figure.

For the sheared cube we have

\[\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(0{,}001 - 0) = 0{,}0005 ,\]

the same as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The entry is positive, so the material turns from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(x\), by the angle \(0{,}0005\) rad: the vertical fibres tilt in the direction of the axis \(x\), and the horizontal ones along the axis \(x\) downwards. The tilt of each edge is the sum of a part from \(\ten\varepsilon\) and a part from \(\ten\omega\), because \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\):

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} + \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005 + 0{,}0005 = 0{,}001 , \\ \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} - \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005 - 0{,}0005 = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

The tilt of the vertical edge \(AD\) by \(0{,}001\) is therefore half shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and half turn \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The bottom edge \(AB\) is tilted upwards by the shear strain by \(0{,}0005\), and the turn tilts it downwards by exactly as much, so it stays horizontal. The right angle at \(A\) decreases by \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}001\) rad, by as much as the edges tilt towards each other because of the shear strain, while the turn does not change it, because it turns both edges equally. So we saw in the split of the cube's matrix in section 1.16: the symmetric part tilts the edges towards each other, the antisymmetric part turns the front face clockwise, and their sum is the shear of the cube.

1.17.6 When the small strain tensor fails

We obtained the small strain tensor by leaving out products of partial derivatives. For this we assumed that all partial derivatives are small, not only the strains. What happens if a body turns a lot but deforms little? Let us take the most extreme case, a body that does not deform at all.

The model is a thin square plate that lies in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) and that we turn as a whole about the axis \(z\), without deforming it. We measure lengths in centimetres, the side of the plate is \(5\), and its corners are \(O = (0, 0, 0)\), \(A = (5, 0, 0)\), \(B = (5, 5, 0)\) and \(C = (0, 5, 0)\). Let us draw it from above, before the turn and after it (figure 1.407).

The axes are \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards. We look at the plate from above, so the axis \(z\) points towards the reader, as the right-hand rule requires: the fingers from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\), the thumb along the axis \(z\) (a right-handed system). The point \(O\) is the centre of the turn. The blackwhite square is the plate before the turn, its corners are \(A\) on the axis \(x\), \(B\) and \(C\). The orange square is the same plate after the turn. It turns as a whole about \(O\), so the corners \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) move to \(A_1\), \(B_1\) and \(C_1\). The blue arc \(\varphi\) is the angle of the turn. The thick blackwhite line \(OA\) is the fibre, \(5\) long, as the dimension \(5\) below it shows. After the turn the fibre \(OA_1\) is the thick orange line. The grey dashed vertical line from \(A_1\) drops to the axis \(x\). The dimension \(3\) below the axis is the component of the fibre along the axis \(x\), and the dimension \(4\) to the right of the vertical line is the height of the point \(A_1\) above the axis \(x\), so \(A_1 = (3, 4, 0)\). The fibre \(OA_1\) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the legs \(3\) and \(4\), so its length is \(\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\), as much as \(OA\), since the plate does not deform. The fibre is turned, so its component along the axis \(x\) decreases from \(5\) to \(3\), which the small strain tensor will read as a shortening by \(40\) %.

From the same triangle we read the angle of the turn. The ratio of the adjacent leg to the hypotenuse, the cosine of the angle \(\varphi\), is \(c = 3/5 = 0{,}6\), and the ratio of the opposite leg to the hypotenuse, the sine of the angle \(\varphi\), is \(s = 4/5 = 0{,}8\). The angle is \(\varphi = 53{,}13^\circ\). Since \(3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2\),

\[c^2 + s^2 = 0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1 .\]

The displacement field of this turn is

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = (c - 1)\,x - s\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = s\,x + (c - 1)\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 , \qquad c = 0{,}6 , \quad s = 0{,}8 .\]

The point \((x, y, z)\) moves to the position \((x + u_{\mathrm{x}},\ y + u_{\mathrm{y}},\ z + u_{\mathrm{z}}) = (c\,x - s\,y,\ s\,x + c\,y,\ z)\). Let us check on two points at distance \(1\) from the axis \(z\):

\[(1, 0, 0) \;\to\; (c,\ s,\ 0) , \qquad (0, 1, 0) \;\to\; (-s,\ c,\ 0) .\]

The first turns by the angle \(\varphi\) from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\), the second by the same angle from the axis \(y\) away from the axis \(x\), and both stay at distance \(\sqrt{c^2 + s^2} = 1\). The corners \(A\) and \(C\) lie five times farther from the axis: the corner \(A\) moves to \(A_1 = (3, 4, 0)\), the corner \(C\) to \(C_1 = (-4, 3, 0)\), and the points on the axis \(z\) do not move.

Is this really a rigid-body displacement (definition 1.11)? Let us check that the distance between no two points changes.

  1. Let the points \(P\) and \(Q\) differ by \((\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)\) before loading, for the fibre \(OA\) by \((5, 0, 0)\). We subtract the new positions coordinate by coordinate.
