Since each new coordinate is a sum of multiples of the old ones, the new positions differ by \((c\,\Delta x - s\,\Delta y,\ s\,\Delta x + c\,\Delta y,\ \Delta z)\).
  2. We multiply out the square of the new distance:
    \[\begin{aligned} (c\,\Delta x - s\,\Delta y)^2 + (s\,\Delta x + c\,\Delta y)^2 + \Delta z^2 &= c^2\Delta x^2 - 2cs\,\Delta x\,\Delta y + s^2\Delta y^2 \\ &\quad + s^2\Delta x^2 + 2sc\,\Delta x\,\Delta y + c^2\Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2 . \end{aligned}\]
  3. The mixed terms cancel, and we collect the others, as for the fibre \(OA_1\) from \((3, 4, 0)\) with \(3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2\): \((c^2 + s^2)(\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2) + \Delta z^2 = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2\), because \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\).

The distances stay the same, the plate does not deform. The fibre \(OA\) of length \(5\) becomes \(OA_1\) with the length \(\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\). What do the two measures of strain say? The displacement gradient is, at every point,

\[\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} c - 1 & -s & 0 \\ s & c - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}4 & -0{,}8 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & -0{,}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat F = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & -0{,}8 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The entry \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is \(0{,}6^2 + 0{,}8^2 + 0^2 = 1\), the entry \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is \(0{,}6 \cdot (-0{,}8) + 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 = 0\), and in the same way we find \(\mat F^\T\mat F = \mat I\). So the Green-Lagrange tensor is exactly zero, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat I - \mat I) = \mat 0\), and it correctly says that no fibre gets longer. The small strain tensor, however, is

\[\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\big(\mat H + \mat H^\T\big) = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -0{,}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

By the formula (1.53), for a fibre in the direction \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) in the plane of the plate we get

\[\varepsilon(\vek n) \approx -0{,}4\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}4\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = -0{,}4\,\big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2\big) = -0{,}4 ,\]

so every fibre in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) would get shorter by \(40\) %, which is false. Where does the error come from? The number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = c - 1 = -0{,}4\) measures only how the component \(x\) of a fibre along the axis \(x\) changes. The fibre \(OA\) turns into \(OA_1\), its component \(x\) decreases from \(5\) to \(3\), but its length stays \(5\). The small strain tensor mistakes the turn for a shortening, because it leaves out the squares of the partial derivatives. The Green-Lagrange tensor keeps them. By (1.48) we have

\[\begin{aligned} E_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac12\bigg[\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}\Big)^2 + \Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big)^2 + \Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big)^2\bigg] \\ &= -0{,}4 + \tfrac12\,\big(0{,}4^2 + 0{,}8^2 + 0\big) = -0{,}4 + 0{,}08 + 0{,}32 = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

The first term is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the other two are the terms that the small strain tensor leaves out, and in a turn together they are exactly as large as the first.

Let us draw the same on a single point and at a smaller angle (figure 1.408).

The axes are \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards, the point \(O\) is on the axis of the turn. The blackwhite segment leads to the point \((1, 0)\), which is at distance \(1\) from the axis. The grey dashed arc is the circle of radius \(1\) along which the point moves, because its distance from the axis does not change. The orange segment leads to the new position \((c, s)\). The dimension \(s\) is the sideways shift of the point, the height of the new position above the axis \(x\). The dimension \(c\) is the new coordinate \(x\), and the dimension \(1 - c\) is the amount by which the coordinate \(x\) decreased. This is the false shortening that the small strain tensor reads as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c - 1\). In the figure the angle is \(30^\circ\), \(s = 0{,}5\) and \(1 - c = 0{,}134\): the decrease of the coordinate is much smaller than the sideways shift and is close to \(s^2/2 = 0{,}125\).

Let us draw the graph. The horizontal axis is \(s\), the sine of the angle of the turn, between \(0\) and \(0{,}1\). The vertical axis is \(1 - c\). The false strain that the small strain tensor assigns to a rigid turn is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c - 1\) and is negative, but in the figure we draw its size \(1 - c\), so that the curve rises upwards. The orange curve shows how the error grows with \(s\). It grows slowly for small \(s\) and faster for larger \(s\), because it is almost equal to \(s^2/2\). The grey dashed horizontal line is the level \(0{,}001\), the strain at which steel already gets permanently longer (section 1.1). The dot at \(s = \sqrt{0{,}002} \approx 0{,}045\), which is an angle of \(2{,}6^\circ\), is the place where the curve reaches this level. The dot at \(s = 0{,}1\), which is an angle of \(5{,}7^\circ\), has the value \(1 - c = 0{,}0050\), five times more.

How large is the error for a small turn? Let us show that the false strain \(c - 1\) is almost exactly \(-s^2/2\), with an error of only about \(s^4/8\). Take \(s = 0{,}001\), which is an angle of \(0{,}057^\circ\), and \(c = \sqrt{1 - s^2}\), so that again \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\) and the displacement is rigid. A point 1 m from the axis moves sideways by about 1 mm. Then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c - 1 = -5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), about \(-s^2/2\). We get the difference of the numbers \(c\) and \(1 - s^2/2\) from the difference of their squares divided by their sum, as in (1.17). Since \(c^2 = 1 - s^2\) and \((1 - s^2/2)^2 = 1 - s^2 + s^4/4\),

\[c - \Big(1 - \frac{s^2}{2}\Big) = \frac{c^2 - (1 - s^2/2)^2}{c + 1 - s^2/2} = \frac{-s^4/4}{c + 1 - s^2/2} .\]

The denominator is almost \(2\), so \(c\) differs from \(1 - s^2/2\) only by about \(s^4/8\), for \(s = 0{,}001\) by \(1{,}25 \cdot 10^{-13}\). The false strain \(c - 1\) is therefore proportional to the square of the turn. For \(s = 0{,}001\) it is small compared with the strains of steel of about \(0{,}001\). For \(s = 0{,}1\), when a point 1 m from the axis moves sideways by about 10 cm, however, \(c - 1 = -0{,}0050\). This is five times the strain at which steel already gets permanently longer, although the body does not deform at all.

How large a turn is still allowed? The false strain \(s^2/2\) must be small compared with the strains we calculate. For strains of about \(0{,}001\), \(s^2/2\) must therefore be much smaller than \(0{,}001\), that is, \(s\) much smaller than \(\sqrt{0{,}002} \approx 0{,}045\). The turn may be larger than the strains, but not arbitrarily large: the limit is of the order of the square root of the strain. This agrees with the estimate of section 1.17.3. There we showed that the small strain tensor underestimates the strain of a fibre by at most \(4{,}5\,m^2\), where \(m\) is the largest absolute value of the partial derivatives of the displacement. Here the partial derivatives are the entries of the matrix \(\mat H\), the numbers \(c - 1\), \(s\) and \(-s\), and the largest in absolute value is \(s\), so \(m = s\). The true error for the fibre \(OA\) is the difference between the true strain \(0\) and the number \(c - 1\), that is, \(1 - c \approx s^2/2\), nine times less than the bound \(4{,}5\,s^2\).

The small strain tensor is therefore a good approximation only when all partial derivatives of the displacements are small, that is, when the strains and also the turns are small. For strains of about \(0{,}001\) the turn \(s = 0{,}01\), which is an angle of \(0{,}57^\circ\), is still small enough: the false strain is \(0{,}00005\), twenty times less than \(0{,}001\). In steel structures the strains are small, and when the turns of their parts are small too, this is so. When parts of a body turn a lot while the body deforms little, the Green-Lagrange tensor must be used. An example is a thin ruler bent into an arc, from section 1.17.3. The ruler is fixed in the wall on the left, and we bend it upwards at the free end. It has the thickness \(t = 1\) mm and the length \(L = 300\) mm. The centre line of the ruler keeps the length \(L\) and becomes an arc of radius \(R\) and central angle equal to the turn of the end, \(\varphi = 30^\circ = \pi/6\). The length of an arc is the radius times the angle in radians, so

\[R = \frac{L}{\varphi} = \frac{300\ \text{mm}}{\pi/6} \approx 573\ \text{mm} .\]

The outer fibres lie \(t/2\) from the centre line, have the radius \(R + t/2\) and the same angle \(\varphi\), so their length is \((R + t/2)\,\varphi = L + \tfrac t2\,\varphi\). Their strain is therefore

\[\frac{(t/2)\,\varphi}{L} = \frac{t}{2R} = \frac{0{,}5\ \text{mm}}{573\ \text{mm}} \approx 0{,}00087 .\]

The strain of the surface is therefore only \(0{,}00087\), while the turn of the end is large, \(s = \sin\varphi = 0{,}5\). For a fibre along the ruler at the end, the small strain tensor would give, because of the turn alone, a false strain \(c - 1 = -0{,}134\), more than a hundred times the true one. The same holds for large deformations, for example in rubber. CM warns that smallness must be checked separately in every application (CM (3.5.16)-(3.5.18), PDF pp. 143-144). The example with the turned plate is not from a source.

The opposite also holds: the small strain tensor can be zero although distances change. Take the field of the small turn from section 1.6, \(\vek u = (-\theta\,y,\ \theta\,x,\ 0)\), for which we got \(\ten\varepsilon = \mat 0\) above. Its displacement gradient has \(-\theta\) and \(\theta\) off the diagonal, so by lemma 1.113 \(\mat E = \ten\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\):

\[\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\theta & 0 \\ \theta & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat E = \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac12\,\theta^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac12\,\theta^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The Green-Lagrange tensor is not zero and is right. A straight line replaces the circular arc in this field, so a point at distance \(1\) from the axis does not move along the circle but along the tangent, and its distance from the axis increases to \(\sqrt{1 + \theta^2}\), as we calculated in section 1.6. For \(\theta = 0{,}1\) every fibre in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) gets longer, the Green-Lagrange quotient is \(\tfrac12\,\theta^2 = 0{,}005\), and the small strain tensor does not detect this.

1.17.7 Strain relative to the shape after loading

The Green-Lagrange strain tensor and the small strain tensor measure fibres that we choose before loading. Let us draw such a fibre before loading and after it (figure 1.410).

The point \(P\) and the point \(Q\) are the end points of the fibre before loading, the blackwhite segment between them is the fibre. The grey dimension below it is its length \(L_0\). The blue arrow beside it is the unit vector \(\vek n\), the direction of the fibre before loading. The arrow is set off from the fibre so that it does not lie on it. After loading the end points move. The grey dimension \(\vek u(P)\) and the grey dimension \(\vek u(Q)\) show by how much, and lead to the point \(P_1\) and the point \(Q_1\). The orange segment between them is the fibre after loading. It is longer and turned, everything is greatly magnified. The grey dimension above it is its length \(L_1\). The blue arrow beside it is the unit vector \(\vek m\), the direction of the fibre after loading.

So far we have taken the point \(P\) and the direction \(\vek n\) on the unloaded body, and compared the change of the square of the length of the fibre with the square of its length before loading, \(L_0^2\). By theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre,

\[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_0^2} = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n .\]

This is how we have described a body ever since section 1.6: we name every point by the position it had before loading and assign to it its displacement. Books call this the Lagrangian or material description (Lagrangeov ali materialni opis).

Sometimes, however, we know a body mainly after loading. So we introduce another measure, which chooses the fibre after loading, and at the end of the section we show when it does not matter which of the two measures we take. First two examples where we see the body only after loading. We draw a grid of short marks on an unloaded rubber band, stretch the band and take a photograph (figure 1.411).

The blackwhite rectangle is the band before loading, the short marks on it are the grid that we drew, all at the same angle. The thick mark is a single short fibre. The orange rectangle is the same band stretched by forces at both ends that pull outwards. It is longer and a little thinner. The orange marks are the same marks after loading: longer and flatter, because the band stretched along its length and shrank across it: in the figure each mark gets longer by the factor \(1{,}8\) along the band and shrinks to \(0{,}6\) across it, so the tilt decreases from \(45^\circ\) to about \(18^\circ\). Such large changes are only for clarity. The thick orange mark is the same fibre as before. On the photograph we see each mark in its position, direction and length after loading, and by these we also choose it.

For a liquid flowing in a pipe, we want to know what happens at a given place in the pipe, not where the bit of liquid that is there now was before. A description in which we name points by their position after loading is the Eulerian or spatial description (Eulerjev ali prostorski opis). CM says that for solid bodies the Eulerian description is less useful, because we do not know the shape of the body after loading in advance, while for the motion of liquids it is the one usually used (CM §3.2.1-§3.2.3, PDF pp. 112-114 and 117).

Let us draw the pipe. Two walls bound the pipe, the arrow above them shows the direction in which the liquid flows. The dashed window is a given place in the pipe, marked \(\vek x\). The window is at rest, the liquid flows through it. The orange bit is the one that is now in the window. The same bit was earlier on the left, at the place \(\vek X\) (grey dashed rectangle), and the grey arrow shows its path to the window. The grey solid bit is another bit that will be in the window later. The Eulerian description asks what is in the window, and names the bit by the place \(\vek x\), not by the place \(\vek X\) where it was before.

The goal of this section is a measure of stretching that compares the change of the square of the length of a short fibre with the square of its length after loading, \(L_1^2\), and gives the direction of the fibre after loading:

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} .\]

We will find a matrix that gives the limit of this quotient for every direction \(\vek m\) after loading, and show how it is related to the Green-Lagrange tensor. Why do we need one more measure? The first reason is measurement: a photograph of a stretched band gives the fibres after loading, their directions \(\vek m\) and lengths \(L_1\), but not the directions \(\vek n\) before loading. The second reason is this book: with the new measure we show when it does not matter whether we choose the fibre before loading or after it. For small partial derivatives it does not, for large deformations it does, and then we must say which measure we use.

The physical model and both assumptions are the same as in the whole of section 1.17: the body is a continuum, its displacement field is continuously differentiable, and the point \(P\) is an interior point of the body. We add one more assumption: the deformation gradient \(\mat F\) at the point \(P\) has an inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\). We will need it because from the fibre after loading we will compute the fibre before it, so we go in the opposite direction from \(\mat F\). What this means physically we said in section 1.16.5 (figure 1.373). Matter cannot be squeezed so that a fibre disappears, and CM concludes from this that the matrix \(\mat F\) is invertible (CM §3.3.1, PDF pp. 119-120). That a matrix which sends no nonzero vector to the zero vector really has an inverse matrix, we will show only in chapter 2. Until then the existence of the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) is an assumption, which we check by calculation in the examples.

Let us start with the bar, where everything is a single number. A bar of length \(L_0\) gets longer, to the length \(L_1\). In section 1.1 we met the Green-Lagrange strain \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\). If we divide the change of the square of the length by the square of the new length, we get the quotient

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} .\]

Let us express it with the strain of the bar \(\varepsilon = (L_1 - L_0)/L_0\).

  1. From the definition of the strain, \(L_1 = L_0\,(1 + \varepsilon)\). The square is a multiplied-out product, \(L_1^2 = L_0^2\,(1 + \varepsilon)(1 + \varepsilon) = L_0^2\,(1 + 2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2)\), as in section 1.6.2.
  2. So the numerator is \(L_1^2 - L_0^2\) \(= L_0^2\,(2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2)\), and the denominator is \(2L_1^2 = 2L_0^2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2\).
  3. The factor \(L_0^2\) cancels:
    \[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \frac{2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} . \tag{1.56}\]
  4. The quotient differs from the strain \(\varepsilon\) by
    \[\varepsilon - \frac{2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} = \frac{2\varepsilon\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2 - 2\varepsilon - \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} = \frac{\varepsilon^2\,(3 + 2\varepsilon)}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} ,\]
    which for small \(\varepsilon\) is almost \(\tfrac32\,\varepsilon^2\). Let us write the right-hand side as \(\varepsilon^2\) times a fraction and look at the fraction:
    \[\frac{3 + 2\varepsilon}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} \;\to\; \frac{3 + 0}{2 \cdot 1} = \frac32 \quad \text{at} \quad \varepsilon \to 0 .\]
    At \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\) the fraction is \(1{,}4980\), almost \(\tfrac32\). We got the numerator by multiplying out \((1 + \varepsilon)^2\) as in step 1 and collecting the terms: \(2\varepsilon + 4\varepsilon^2 + 2\varepsilon^3 - 2\varepsilon - \varepsilon^2 = 3\varepsilon^2 + 2\varepsilon^3\). The Green-Lagrange strain \(\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), on the other hand, differs from \(\varepsilon\) by \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\).

For a steel bar with \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\) the new quotient is \(0{,}0009985\) and the Green-Lagrange strain \(0{,}0010005\). The first differs from \(\varepsilon\) by one and a half per mille of its value, the second by half a per mille. For a rubber band stretched from 10 cm to 15 cm, \(\varepsilon = 0{,}5\), the new quotient is \((15^2 - 10^2)/(2 \cdot 15^2) = 125/450 = 0{,}278\) and the Green-Lagrange strain \(0{,}625\) (figure 1.413). In order of size they follow each other as follows:

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = 0{,}278 \;<\; \varepsilon = 0{,}5 \;<\; \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_0^2} = 0{,}625 .\]

For large strains the measures differ a lot.

Let us draw the graph. The horizontal axis is the ratio of lengths \(L_1/L_0\) from \(0{,}5\) to \(2\), the vertical axis is the value of the measure. The blackwhite straight line is the strain \(\varepsilon = L_1/L_0 - 1\). The blue curve is the Green-Lagrange strain \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\). The orange curve is the quotient \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\), which divides the change of the square of the length by the square of the length after loading. The dot at \(L_1/L_0 = 1\) is the common point of all three, where the fibre is not stretched and all three are zero. There they have the same slope, so for small strains they almost agree. For larger ratios they diverge, and the blackwhite line always lies between the curves. The three dots at \(L_1/L_0 = 1{,}5\) are the values for the rubber band stretched from 10 cm to 15 cm: \(0{,}5\), \(0{,}625\) and \(0{,}278\). The three dots at \(L_1/L_0 = 2\) are the values for a stretch to double the length: \(1\), \(1{,}5\) and \(0{,}375\). The three dots at \(L_1/L_0 = 0{,}5\) lie on the vertical axis, because the graph starts there. These are the values for shortening to a half: \(\varepsilon = -0{,}5\), the Green-Lagrange strain \((0{,}25 - 1)/2 = -0{,}375\) and the new quotient \((0{,}25 - 1)/(2 \cdot 0{,}25) = -1{,}5\), which is written next to the axis. For shortening, the new quotient is the largest in size of the three, so the orange curve drops lowest on the left.

Why is the new quotient always smaller than the Green-Lagrange one when the length changes? Both have the same numerator \(L_1^2 - L_0^2\). When the bar is stretched, \(L_1 > L_0\), so the new quotient divides a positive numerator by a larger number and is smaller. When the bar gets shorter, \(L_1 < L_0\), and the new quotient divides a negative numerator by a smaller number, so it is larger in size and again smaller. The strain \(\varepsilon\) always lies between the two. The Green-Lagrange strain is larger than it by \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), and the new quotient is smaller by step 4, because a bar cannot disappear, so \(L_1 > 0\), \(\varepsilon > -1\) and \(3 + 2\varepsilon > 0\).

The new quotient has one more meaning. We let the stretched band of length 15 cm go back to 10 cm, and we take the length of the stretched band as the initial length. The Green-Lagrange strain of this unloading is \((10^2 - 15^2)/(2 \cdot 15^2) = -0{,}278\), the new quotient with the opposite sign. This is always so: when we swap the roles of the lengths \(L_0\) and \(L_1\), the Green-Lagrange quotient becomes \((L_0^2 - L_1^2)/(2L_1^2)\), which is the new quotient with the opposite sign. So the new quotient measures stretching with the length seen by someone who knows only the loaded body.

In space we proceed as in section 1.17.2 and first leave out the remainders, which we will justify in the theorem below. A remainder is the difference between the true vector of the fibre after loading and the vector given by the deformation gradient. A fibre from the point \(P\) in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n\) with length \(h > 0\) has after loading, by lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading and without the remainders, the vector \(\mat F\,(h\,\vek n) = h\,\mat F\vek n\) (the fibre after loading in figure 1.410).

  1. Its length after loading is \(L_1 \approx h\,|\mat F\vek n|\). The vector \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, as we will show in the theorem below, so we may divide it by its length. We get the unit vector \(\vek m = \mat F\vek n / |\mat F\vek n|\), the direction of the fibre after loading. The vector of the fibre after loading is thus \(h\,\mat F\vek n \approx L_1\,\vek m\).
  2. We express the vector of the fibre before loading with the vector after loading. Since \(\mat F^{-1}\mat F = \mat I\) ((1.43)), \(\mat F^{-1}(h\,\mat F\vek n) = h\,(\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = h\,\vek n\). We may combine the factors like this by lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product. So \(h\,\vek n \approx L_1\,\mat F^{-1}\vek m\). The matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) takes the vector of the fibre after loading back to the vector before loading, just as for the sheared cube the matrix \(\mat I - \mat K\) took back the edge \(AD\) (section 1.16.5). There \(\mat K\) is the displacement gradient \(\mat H\) of the cube.
  3. So the square of the length before loading is \(L_0^2 = h^2 \approx L_1^2\,|\mat F^{-1}\vek m|^2\). We expand the square of the length of the vector \(\vek w = \mat F^{-1}\vek m\) just like \(|\mat F\vek n|^2\) in section 1.17.2. The component \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) is row \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) multiplied by \(\vek m\), so
    \[\begin{aligned} |\vek w|^2 &= \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}^2 \\ &= \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} (\mat F^{-1})_{\mathrm{ki}}\,m_{\mathrm{i}}\Big)\Big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat F^{-1})_{\mathrm{kj}}\,m_{\mathrm{j}}\Big) \\ &= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} m_{\mathrm{i}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} (\mat F^{-1})_{\mathrm{ki}}\,(\mat F^{-1})_{\mathrm{kj}}\Big)\,m_{\mathrm{j}} . \end{aligned}\]
    The sum in the brackets is the entry in row \(\ix{i}\) and column \(\ix{j}\) of the matrix \((\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\), because \((\mat F^{-1})_{\mathrm{ki}}\) is the entry in row \(\ix{i}\) and column \(\ix{k}\) of the transposed matrix. The double sum is therefore
    \[|\mat F^{-1}\vek m|^2 = \vek m^\T\,(\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\,\vek m .\]
  4. We will subtract the squares of the lengths, so we also write \(L_1^2\) as a double sum with the vector \(\vek m\). The vector \(\vek m\) is a unit vector, so \(1 = \vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m\) as in step 6 there (only the terms with equal indices remain), and \(L_1^2 = L_1^2\,\vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m\).
  5. We subtract the squares of the lengths, divide by \(2L_1^2\) and subtract the two double sums term by term:
    \[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} \approx \frac{L_1^2\,\vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m - L_1^2\,\vek m^\T(\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\vek m}{2L_1^2} = \vek m^\T\,\tfrac12\big(\mat I - (\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\big)\,\vek m .\]

On the right there is again a single matrix, which depends only on the displacement field at the point \(P\), and the direction appears only in the vector \(\vek m\), this time in the direction of the fibre after loading. The matrix contains the transposed matrix of the inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\). Before we give the matrix a name, let us show that this is the same matrix as the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\). That way we may denote both by one symbol, and above all in the proof of lemma 1.119 we will need the product of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) with this matrix to be the identity matrix.

Let us draw what the lemma says on the sheared cube. Top left is the matrix \(\mat F^\T\), in which \(0{,}001\) is now in row \(z\) and column \(x\). The arrow leads to its inverse matrix, in which this entry is \(-0{,}001\). Bottom left is the inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) of the cube, with \(-0{,}001\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\). The arrow leads to its transposed matrix, where \(-0{,}001\) is again in row \(z\) and column \(x\). The sign \(=\) says that the two right matrices are equal, which is what the lemma states.

Lemma 1.117 Inverse of the transposed matrix (inverzna matrika transponirane matrike)

Let a square matrix \(\mat A\) of order \(n\) have an inverse matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\). Then the transposed matrix \(\mat A^\T\) also has an inverse matrix, and it is the transposed matrix of the matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\):

\[(\mat A^\T)^{-1} = (\mat A^{-1})^\T .\]
Proof

We must show that the matrix \((\mat A^{-1})^\T\) satisfies both equalities of definition 1.107 for the matrix \(\mat A^\T\).

  1. We write \(\mat B = \mat A^{-1}\). By (1.43), \(\mat A\mat B = \mat I\) and \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\).
  2. We transpose the first equality. By item 3 of lemma 1.101, \((\mat A\mat B)^\T = \mat B^\T\mat A^\T\), so \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T = \mat I^\T\).
  3. The identity matrix equals its transposed matrix. The entry \((\ix{i}, \ix{j})\) of the matrix \(\mat I^\T\) is \(I_{\mathrm{ji}}\) (definition 1.100), which is \(1\) for \(\ix{j} = \ix{i}\) and \(0\) otherwise, the same as \(I_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 1.105). So \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T = \mat I\).
  4. In the same way we transpose the second equality, \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\), and get \(\mat A^\T\mat B^\T = \mat I\).
  5. The matrices \(\mat A^\T\) and \(\mat B^\T\) are square matrices of order \(n\), and by steps 3 and 4 they satisfy both equalities (1.43) with \(\mat A^\T\) in the place of the matrix \(\mat A\). So \(\mat B^\T\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat A^\T\). By lemma 1.108 on the uniqueness of the inverse matrix there is no other, so \((\mat A^\T)^{-1} = \mat B^\T = (\mat A^{-1})^\T\).

Source: CM §2.3.6 (PDF p. 65) states the equality without proof, KREYSZIG §7.8, problems 13 and 14 (PDF p. 335), leaves its check and proof to the reader. The proof is not from the sources.

So we write the matrix \((\mat A^{-1})^\T = (\mat A^\T)^{-1}\) more briefly as \(\mat A^{-\T}\), as CM does (CM §2.3.6, PDF p. 65). The proof used only the rule for transposing a product, the fact that the identity matrix equals its transposed matrix, and the uniqueness of the inverse matrix. For the sheared cube \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) (section 1.16.5), so by item 2 of lemma 1.101 and step 3 above, \(\mat F^{-\T} = \mat I^\T - \mat K^\T = \mat I - \mat K^\T\). This is the matrix that has a single nonzero entry off the main diagonal, \(-0{,}001\) in row \(z\) and column \(x\).

Definition 1.118 Euler-Almansi strain tensor (Euler-Almansijev tenzor deformacij)

Let \(\mat F\) be the deformation gradient at an interior point \(P\) of a body, and let \(\mat F\) have an inverse matrix. The Euler-Almansi strain tensor (Euler-Almansijev tenzor deformacij) at the point \(P\) is the matrix

\[\mat E^* = \tfrac12\big(\mat I - \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\big) , \tag{1.57}\]

where \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat F^{-1})^\T\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) (lemma 1.117). We denote its entry in row \(\ix{i}\) and column \(\ix{j}\) by \(E^*_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Source: CM (3.4.24) (PDF p. 133), BOWER §2.1.6 (PDF p. 49).

What kind of object is \(\mat E^*\)? Like \(\mat E\), it is a \(3 \times 3\) matrix, calculated from the deformation gradient at one point. It is symmetric (definition 1.102). By items 3 and 1 of lemma 1.101, \((\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1})^\T = (\mat F^{-1})^\T(\mat F^{-\T})^\T = \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\), and the identity matrix equals its transposed matrix, so by item 2 of the same lemma \((\mat E^*)^\T = \mat E^*\). The matrix \(\mat E^*\) therefore has at most six different entries. We calculate it from the partial derivatives of the displacements at the point \(P\), but its numbers describe the fibres that pass through the point \(P_1\) after loading, in their directions after loading.

In the sources this tensor has different names and symbols. BOWER calls it the Eulerian strain tensor (Eulerjev tenzor deformacij) and denotes it by \(\mat E^*\) (BOWER §2.1.6, PDF p. 49). CM calls it the Almansi-Hamel or Euler strain tensor (Almansi-Hamelov ali Eulerjev tenzor deformacij), and in its examples the Almansi strain tensor, and writes it with a small bold \(\mathbf e\) (CM, PDF pp. 133-134). The name in this book joins the two names. Anyone who reads CM should also know this: CM also writes it with partial derivatives of the displacements with respect to the coordinates of the points after loading, and there the quadratic part has the opposite sign to that of the Green-Lagrange tensor (CM (3.4.25) and (3.4.27), PDF p. 133). We will not use such derivatives, because we name the points of a body by their position before loading.

Let us calculate \(\mat E^*\) right away on the sheared cube, which is glued to the table by its bottom face and whose top face we pushed sideways by \(s = 10\) µm at the height \(h = 10\,000\) µm. The axis \(x\) points in the direction of the push, the axis \(z\) upward. The displacement gradient of the cube \(\mat K\) has a single nonzero entry, \(0{,}001\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\), because \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\). Let us write it on the board together with the deformation gradient and its inverse matrix from section 1.16.5:

\[\begin{aligned} \mat K &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \\ \mat F &= \mat I + \mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \\ \mat F^{-1} &= \mat I - \mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} . \end{aligned}\]

Above we also got \(\mat F^{-\T} = \mat I - \mat K^\T\). We do the calculation in three steps (figure 1.415).

At the top are the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) and the matrix \(\mat K\), which we will multiply. The middle row will hold the sum of three matrices, the bottom one the result. Each step below shows which part of the figure does the calculation.

  1. We multiply out the brackets term by term by item 3 of lemma 1.99 and lemma 1.106: \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = (\mat I - \mat K^\T)(\mat I - \mat K) = \mat I - \mat K - \mat K^\T + \mat K^\T\mat K\), where \(\mat K\), \(\mat K^\T\) and \(\mat K^\T\mat K\) are the matrices in the figure.
  2. In the product \(\mat K^\T\mat K\) only the entry in row \(z\) and column \(z\) is nonzero. Row \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) is \((0{,}001, 0, 0)\), column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is also \((0{,}001, 0, 0)\), and their product is \(0{,}001^2 = 10^{-6}\). The other rows of the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) and the other columns of the matrix \(\mat K\) are zero.
  3. By (1.57), therefore, the half of the sum of three matrices, the matrix \(\mat E^*\), is
    \[\mat E^* = \tfrac12\big(\mat K + \mat K^\T - \mat K^\T\mat K\big) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & -0{,}0000005 \end{bmatrix} .\]
    The entries \(xz\) and \(zx\) are \(0{,}0005\), the same as for the small strain tensor, and the entry \(zz\) is \(-5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), the product of the partial derivatives \(0{,}001 \cdot 0{,}001\) divided by \(-2\).

Both matrices, \(\mat E\) and \(\mat E^*\), are calculated from the same matrix \(\mat F\). How do we get one from the other?

Let us draw the diagram. In the top row, on the left, is the blackwhite arrow \(\vek n\), the direction of the fibre before loading. On the right is the orange arrow \(\vek m\), the direction of the same fibre after loading. The upper blue arrow in the top row leads from \(\vek n\) towards \(\vek m\). It says exactly what the matrix \(\mat F\) does: it sends the vector \(\vek n\) to the vector \(\mat F\vek n = |\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m\), which has the direction \(\vek m\) but the length \(|\mat F\vek n|\), not \(1\). Only when we divide it by its length do we get \(\vek m\). The lower arrow in the top row leads back: \(\mat F^{-1}\) sends \(\vek m\) to a vector with the direction \(\vek n\) and the length \(|\mat F^{-1}\vek m|\). In the bottom row, on the left, is the blackwhite rectangle with \(\mat E\), the Green-Lagrange measure, and on the right the orange rectangle with \(\mat E^*\), the Euler-Almansi measure. The colours follow the top row: blackwhite before loading, orange after it. The upper arrow in the bottom row says that from \(\mat E\) we get \(\mat E^*\) with the matrices \(\mat F^{-\T}\) from the left and \(\mat F^{-1}\) from the right. The lower arrow in the bottom row leads back, with \(\mat F^\T\) from the left and \(\mat F\) from the right. Under the rectangles are the numbers of the same fibre: \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) for the Green-Lagrange measure and \(A = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\) for the Euler-Almansi one.

Lemma 1.119 Relation between the Euler-Almansi and the Green-Lagrange strain tensor (zveza med Euler-Almansijevim in Green-Lagrangeovim tenzorjem)

Let the deformation gradient \(\mat F\) at an interior point \(P\) of a body have an inverse matrix, and let \(\mat E\) be the Green-Lagrange and \(\mat E^*\) the Euler-Almansi strain tensor at \(P\). Then

\[\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \mat E \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mat E^* = \mat F^{-\T}\mat E\,\mat F^{-1} . \tag{1.58}\]
Proof

We must show both equalities. We use the properties of the matrix product (lemma 1.99) and the fact that \(\mat F^{-\T}\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) (lemma 1.117).

The first equality.

  1. We substitute (1.57). By item 3 of lemma 1.99, used for multiplication from the left and from the right, \(\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \tfrac12\big(\mat F^\T\mat I\,\mat F - \mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\mat F\big)\). In the figure this is the first row: each matrix is a box, in the same order as in the product.
  2. By lemma 1.106, \(\mat F^\T\mat I\,\mat F = \mat F^\T\mat F\). In the second row the identity matrix is drawn grey and dashed, because it drops out, and an arrow leads to what remains.
  3. By item 2 of lemma 1.99, \(\mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\mat F = (\mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T})(\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\). By (1.43) both brackets equal \(\mat I\), the first because \(\mat F^{-\T}\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\). By lemma 1.106, \(\mat I\mat I = \mat I\). In the third row the grey curly brackets under the pairs show which pair gives \(\mat I\).
  4. So \(\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \tfrac12(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I)\), which by (1.47) is the matrix \(\mat E\), as the fourth row shows.

The second equality.

  1. We multiply the first equality from the left by \(\mat F^{-\T}\) and from the right by \(\mat F^{-1}\): \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat E\,\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\mat F^{-1}\). This is the last row, where the grey brackets above the pairs again show which pair gives \(\mat I\).
  2. By item 2 of lemma 1.99 the right side equals \((\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^\T)\,\mat E^*\,(\mat F\mat F^{-1})\). By (1.43) both brackets equal \(\mat I\), and by lemma 1.106, \(\mat I\,\mat E^*\,\mat I = \mat E^*\).

Source: The definitions of the two tensors are CM (3.4.10) (PDF p. 129) and (3.4.24) (PDF p. 133). The proof is not from the sources.

So we get \(\mat E^*\) from \(\mat E\) by multiplying \(\mat E\) from the left by \(\mat F^{-\T}\) and from the right by \(\mat F^{-1}\), and \(\mat E\) from \(\mat E^*\) with the matrices \(\mat F^\T\) and \(\mat F\). When \(\mat E = \mat 0\), therefore also \(\mat E^* = \mat 0\), because every entry of a product with the zero matrix is a sum of products with zero, and the other way round. The proof used only the grouping of factors and the fact that the product of a matrix with its inverse matrix gives the identity matrix.

So far we have left out the remainders. As for the Green-Lagrange tensor, let us show that this is justified for ever shorter fibres. We will not need a new calculation with remainders, because the new quotient is expressed through the Green-Lagrange one.

Let us draw the vectors the theorem is made of. The point \(P\) is the common start of all three vectors. The blackwhite arrow \(\vek n\) is the unit vector of the fibre before loading. The blue arrow \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is the vector to which \(\mat F\) sends it, the fibre after loading at \(h = 1\) without the remainders. For the picture the length \(|\mat F\,\vek n| = 1{,}4\) is chosen, longer than \(1\), because the fibre gets longer. The orange arrow \(\vek m\) lies on the first part of \(\mat F\,\vek n\) and has length \(1\), since it is the unit vector in the direction of \(\mat F\,\vek n\), \(\vek m = \mat F\vek n / |\mat F\vek n|\). So the orange arrow turns into the blue one.

Theorem 1.120 Strain of a short fibre relative to its length after loading (deformacija kratkega vlakna glede na dolžino po obremenitvi)

Let the displacement field of a body be continuously differentiable, \(P\) an interior point of the body, \(r > 0\) a number such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) are interior points of the body (such an \(r\) exists by lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point), \(\mat F\) the deformation gradient at \(P\), which has an inverse matrix, \(\mat E\) the Green-Lagrange and \(\mat E^*\) the Euler-Almansi strain tensor at \(P\), and \(\vek n\) a unit vector. For a number \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r\) let the fibre reach from \(P\) to the point \(Q\) with \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek n\), and let \(P_1\) and \(Q_1\) be the positions of the points \(P\) and \(Q\) after loading. The length of the fibre before loading is \(L_0 = |h|\), and after loading \(L_1 = |\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1}|\). Then \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, and for the unit vector \(\vek m = \mat F\vek n / |\mat F\vek n|\):

  1. the quotient \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\) is defined for all small enough \(|h|\) and approaches the number \(\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\),
    \[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m , \tag{1.59}\]
  2. the two measures are related by the equality
    \[\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = \frac{\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n}{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n} . \tag{1.60}\]
Proof

First we show that \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, then item 2, and from it item 1.

The vector \(\mat F\vek n\).

Let us draw why \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector. Suppose it is. In the figure the vectors are full arrows, while the blue dashed arrows are not vectors: they mean that we multiply by the matrix written beside them. The vector \(\vek n\) of length \(1\) goes by the matrix \(\mat F\) (blue dashed arrow) to the zero vector. By the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) we send it on and again get the zero vector. But the two matrices in a row are \(\mat F^{-1}\mat F = \mat I\) (lower arrow) and return the vector \(\vek n\) of length \(1\). Zero and a vector of length \(1\) are not equal, which is a contradiction.

  1. Suppose that \(\mat F\vek n = \vek 0\).
  2. Then by item 1 of lemma 1.99, \((\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = \mat F^{-1}(\mat F\vek n) = \mat F^{-1}\vek 0\), and every entry of the product \(\mat F^{-1}\vek 0\) is a sum of products with zero, so it is zero.
  3. By (1.43) and lemma 1.106, however, \((\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = \mat I\vek n = \vek n\), which is not the zero vector, because its length is \(1\). This contradicts step 2.
  4. So \(\mat F\vek n \neq \vek 0\), and its length \(|\mat F\vek n|\) is positive. Every component of the vector \(\vek m\) is a component of the vector \(\mat F\vek n\) divided by \(|\mat F\vek n|\), so by (1.10) \(|\vek m|^2 = |\mat F\vek n|^2/|\mat F\vek n|^2 = 1\), and \(\vek m\) is a unit vector.

2. The relation between the two measures.

  1. We write \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\). By step 4 of the proof of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, \(|\mat F\vek n|^2 = \vek n^\T\mat F^\T\mat F\,\vek n\) and \(G = \tfrac12\big(|\mat F\vek n|^2 - 1\big)\). So \(|\mat F\vek n|^2 = 1 + 2G\), and by step 4 above this number is positive (figure 1.420).

Let us draw this for the fibre with length \(|\mat F\vek n| = 1{,}4\) from the figure above, for which \(1 + 2G = 1{,}4^2 = 1{,}96\) and \(G = 0{,}48\). We compare the squares of the lengths at \(h = 1\) on one line. The grey dashed horizontal line is this line. The upper dimension \(L_1^2\) is the square of the length after loading, \(1{,}96\), and the dimension \(L_0^2\) below it is the square of the length before it, \(1\). The grey vertical lines carry the ends of the dimensions to the line, so that the difference between them can be seen. The orange dimension at the bottom is the difference \(L_1^2 - L_0^2 = 2G = 0{,}96\). Below it are the quotients that divide this same difference by different numbers: \(G\) by \(2L_0^2\) and \(A\) by \(2L_1^2\). So \(A = 0{,}48/1{,}96 \approx 0{,}245\), which is \(G/(1 + 2G)\). The steps below show that this holds for every \(\mat F\).

  1. By lemma 1.119, \(\mat E = \mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\), so \(G = \vek n^\T\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\,\vek n\).
  2. By item 3 of lemma 1.101, \(\vek n^\T\mat F^\T = (\mat F\vek n)^\T\), and by item 2 of lemma 1.99 we may group the factors as we like. So \(G = (\mat F\vek n)^\T\,\mat E^*\,(\mat F\vek n)\).
  3. We substitute \(\mat F\vek n = |\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m\). By item 2 of lemma 1.101, \((|\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m)^\T = |\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m^\T\), and by item 3 of lemma 1.99 we take the number out of each product. We get \(G = |\mat F\vek n|^2\,\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = (1 + 2G)\,\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\).
  4. We divide by the positive number \(1 + 2G\) and get (1.60).

1. The limit.

  1. We write \(g(h) = (L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\) and \(c = 1 + 2G\), where \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) as above. By item 1 of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} g(h) = G\), and by step 1 of item 2, \(c = |\mat F\vek n|^2 > 0\).
  2. From the definition of the function \(g\) we get \(L_1^2/L_0^2 = 1 + 2g(h)\), when we multiply the equality \(g(h) = \tfrac12\big(L_1^2/L_0^2 - 1\big)\) by \(2\) and add \(1\).
  3. We use the definition of the limit 1.5 with the error \(c/4\): there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - G| < c/4\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_1\). We may always narrow the band, as we said after the definition of the limit, so we take \(\delta_1 \le r\), and \(g(h)\) is defined for all these \(h\). For such \(h\), \(1 + 2g(h) = c + 2\big(g(h) - G\big) > c - c/2 = c/2\). So \(L_1^2 = L_0^2\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big) > 0\), hence \(L_1 > 0\), and the quotient \(a(h) = (L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\) is defined. So we may apply the definition of the limit to the function \(a\), with \(\delta_1\) in the role of the number \(r\).

Let us draw what step 3 gave, with the number \(c = 2\) for the picture. At the top is the band of the number \(1 + 2g(h)\) around \(c\), of half-width \(c/2\): because \(1 + 2g(h) = c + 2\big(g(h) - G\big)\) and \(|g(h) - G| < c/4\), the number \(1 + 2g(h)\) differs from \(c\) by less than \(c/2\). The left edge of the band, \(c/2\), is therefore a lower bound for the number \(1 + 2g(h)\), and this bound is positive. We will draw the lower half of the figure in steps 6 and 7.

  1. For these \(h\) we divide the numerator and the denominator of the quotient \(a(h)\) by \(L_0^2\) and use step 2:
    \[a(h) = \frac{(L_1^2 - L_0^2)/L_0^2}{2L_1^2/L_0^2} = \frac{2g(h)}{2\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)} = \frac{g(h)}{1 + 2g(h)} .\]
  2. By item 2, \(\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = G/(1 + 2G) = G/c\). We bring the two fractions to a common denominator:
    \[a(h) - \frac{G}{c} = \frac{g(h)\,(1 + 2G) - G\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)}{\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)\,c} = \frac{g(h) - G}{\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)\,c} ,\]
    because the terms \(2\,g(h)\,G\) in the numerator cancel.
  3. By step 3 the denominator is larger than \((c/2) \cdot c = c^2/2\), so \(|a(h) - G/c| < 2\,|g(h) - G|/c^2\). In the figure below this is the factor \(2/c^2\), with which we carry the difference \(g(h) - G\) into the difference \(a(h) - G/c\).
  4. We choose any error \(\eta > 0\). By the definition of the limit there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - G| < \eta\,c^2/2\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_2\), which is the band for \(g(h) - G\) with half-width \(\eta\,c^2/2\) in the figure below. For \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\). For every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\), by step 6, \(|a(h) - G/c| < 2 \cdot (\eta\,c^2/2)/c^2 = \eta\), the band for \(a(h) - G/c\) with half-width \(\eta\), at \(c = 2\) half as wide as the band for \(g(h) - G\). We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so the limit of the quotient \(a(h)\) is \(G/c = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\).

Source: BOWER §2.1.6 (PDF p. 49) writes item 1 for an infinitesimally short fibre, with the unit vector along the fibre after loading and without a limit, and leaves the proof to the reader. CM (3.4.23) (PDF p. 133) writes \((ds)^2 - (dS)^2 = 2\,d\vek x\cdot\mat E^*\cdot d\vek x\). The proof is not from the sources.

The theorem is the version in space of the quotient for the bar. The Euler-Almansi tensor gives, for every direction \(\vek m\) after loading, how much a short fibre has been stretched, measured with its length after loading. The vector \(\vek m\) is the direction of the fibre after loading up to the remainders, since by lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading the vector of the fibre after loading is \(h\,\mat F\vek n\) plus the remainders. For negative \(h\) the fibre points in the direction \(-\vek m\), which does not change the double sum, because each of its terms is a product of two components of the direction. The proof showed why the theorem holds. The new quotient is exactly the Green-Lagrange quotient \(g\) divided by \(1 + 2g = L_1^2/L_0^2\), so we got its limit from theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, and item 2 is the same relation in the limit.

Item 2 relates the two measures of the same fibre. We write \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) and \(A = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\). From (1.60),

\[G - A = G - \frac{G}{1 + 2G} = \frac{G\,(1 + 2G) - G}{1 + 2G} = \frac{2G^2}{1 + 2G} = 2\,G\,A .\]

So the two measures of the same fibre differ by exactly twice their product. When \(|G| \le 0{,}001\), the difference is at most \(0{,}002\,|A|\) in size, two thousandths of the value \(A\). For small strains it therefore does not matter which of the two measures we use. With the strain of the fibre \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) of section 1.17.3 the relation is even simpler. By item 2 of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, the ratio of lengths in the limit is \(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n)\), so

\[\frac{L_1^2}{L_0^2} \to 1 + 2G = \big(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n)\big)^2 .\]

From this \(G = \varepsilon(\vek n) + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2\) and \(A = G/\big(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n)\big)^2\), which is exactly the formula (1.56) with \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\vek n)\). So the curves of figure 1.413 hold for every short fibre, not only for the bar.

Let us test everything on the sheared cube, which is glued to the table by its bottom face and whose top face we pushed sideways by \(s = 10\) µm at the height \(h = 10\,000\) µm. We calculated its Euler-Almansi tensor right away from definition 1.118:

\[\mat E^* = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & -0{,}0000005 \end{bmatrix} .\]

Let us compare it with the Green-Lagrange tensor of the cube from section 1.17.2,

\[\mat E = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & 0{,}0000005 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The matrices differ only in the entry in row \(z\) and column \(z\), which has the opposite sign. How can \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) be positive and \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\) negative? By theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, the entry \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the measure of the fibre that is vertical before loading (\(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\)), and by theorem 1.120 the entry \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the measure of the fibre that is vertical after loading (\(\vek m = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\)). These are two different fibres (figure 1.422).

Let us draw the left half. The axes show \(x\) to the right and \(z\) upwards. The hatched line is the table to which the cube is glued. The thin blackwhite square is the front face before loading, the thin orange parallelogram after it, since we push the top edge by \(s\) to the right. The ratio \(s/h = 0{,}001\) is magnified in the figure to \(0{,}25\) so that the difference can be seen. The corners \(B\), \(C\) and \(C_1\) are labelled at the sides. The thick blackwhite line is the fibre \(AD\), which is vertical before loading, and the thick orange line from \(A\) to \(D_1\) is the same fibre after it: it leans and gets longer. The dimension \(h\) is the height of the cube, the dimension \(s\) is the shift of the top edge. This fibre belongs to the entry \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) of the Green-Lagrange tensor.

The right half shows the same faces. The table, the blackwhite square, the orange parallelogram and the corners are as before. Now we choose another fibre. The thick blackwhite line from \(B\) to \(T\) is the fibre before loading, which is leaning. We choose the point \(T\) so that the fibre is vertical after loading: from \(B\) it goes straight up, to the position \(T_1\) where the corner \(C\) was before loading. The vector of this fibre after loading is \((0, 0, h)\), and the vector of the same fibre before loading is given by the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\), as in step 2 of the derivation above: \(\mat F^{-1}(0, 0, h) = (-0{,}001\,h,\ 0,\ h) = (-s, 0, h)\). So the point \(T\) is on the top edge, \(s\) to the left of \(C\), and after loading it moves by \(s\) to the right, to \(T_1\). So the thick orange line from \(B\) to \(T_1\) is vertical and shorter. This fibre belongs to the entry \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\) of the Euler-Almansi tensor. The dimension \(h\) and the dimension \(s\) are drawn again on the right half, for the same quantities.

The vertical edge \(AD\) leans and gets longer from \(h\) to \(\sqrt{h^2 + s^2} = 10\,000{,}005\) µm. The fibre \(BT\) with coordinates \(B = (10\,000, 0, 0)\), \(T = (9\,990, 0, 10\,000)\) and \(T_1 = (10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) in µm stands upright and gets shorter from \(\sqrt{h^2 + s^2} = 10\,000{,}005\) µm to \(h = 10\,000\) µm. Its quotient is

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \frac{h^2 - (h^2 + s^2)}{2h^2} = -\frac{s^2}{2h^2} = -5 \cdot 10^{-7} ,\]

exactly \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The shear that makes a vertical fibre lean and get longer makes a leaning fibre stand upright and get shorter.

The field of the cube is linear, so there are no remainders, and the equalities of theorem 1.120 hold for every fibre of the cube without a limit, as we saw for the Green-Lagrange tensor in section 1.17.2. Let us calculate both quotients for the fibres of the front face from section 1.6.2 and for the fibre \(BT\), from the lengths in micrometres.

fibre \(L_0\) \(L_1\) \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\) \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\)
bottom edge \(AB\) \(10\,000\) \(10\,000\) \(0\) \(0\)
vertical edge \(AD\) \(10\,000\) \(10\,000{,}005\) \(5{,}000000 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(4{,}999995 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
diagonal \(AC\) \(14\,142{,}136\) \(14\,149{,}208\) \(5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
diagonal \(BD\) \(14\,142{,}136\) \(14\,135{,}066\) \(-4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(-5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
fibre \(BT\) \(10\,000{,}005\) \(10\,000\) \(-4{,}999995 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(-5{,}000000 \cdot 10^{-7}\)

The two columns differ by \(2GA\), as the relation above says. For the diagonals this is \(2 \cdot 5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4} = 5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), which is exactly the difference \(5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4} - 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\). For the edge \(AD\) and the fibre \(BT\) it is only \(2 \cdot (5 \cdot 10^{-7})^2 = 5 \cdot 10^{-13}\), so the columns differ only by a millionth of the value. We also get the last column from the matrix \(\mat E^*\) when we put in the direction of the fibre after loading. For the diagonal \(AC\) the vector after loading is \((10\,010, 0, 10\,000)\) with the length \(14\,149{,}208\) µm, so \(\vek m = (0{,}70746, 0, 0{,}70675)\). Only the terms with the indices \(x\) and \(z\) remain in the double sum:

\[\begin{aligned} \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m &= 2E^*_{\mathrm{xz}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{z}} + E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\,m_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = 2 \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot 0{,}70746 \cdot 0{,}70675 - 5 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 0{,}70675^2 \\ &= 5{,}0000 \cdot 10^{-4} - 2{,}4975 \cdot 10^{-7} = 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4} , \end{aligned}\]

as in the table.

For the plate that in section 1.17.6 we turned as a whole about the axis \(z\) with the numbers \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\), \(\mat F^\T\mat F = \mat I\). Also \(\mat F\mat F^\T = \mat I\). The entry \((\mat F\mat F^\T)_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F\), \((0{,}6, -0{,}8, 0)\), multiplied by column \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\), which is the same triple, so \(0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\). The entry \((\mat F\mat F^\T)_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is \(0{,}6 \cdot 0{,}8 + (-0{,}8) \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 = 0\), and we get the others in the same way. So by definition 1.107 the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F\), and by lemma 1.108 on the uniqueness of the inverse matrix, \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^\T\). Transposing twice gives back the original matrix (lemma 1.101, item 1), so \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat F^\T)^\T = \mat F\). Then \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = \mat F\mat F^\T = \mat I\) and \(\mat E^* = \tfrac12(\mat I - \mat I) = \mat 0\). Like the Green-Lagrange tensor, the Euler-Almansi tensor correctly says that no fibre gets longer, while the small strain tensor wrongly predicts a shortening by \(40\) %. The same follows from lemma 1.119, since \(\mat E = \mat 0\) gives \(\mat E^* = \mat F^{-\T}\,\mat 0\,\mat F^{-1} = \mat 0\).

For the hanging bar all partial derivatives are small. A steel bar 10 m long hangs under its own weight and is fixed only at the point \(O\), the centre of its upper end, the axis \(x\) points vertically down, and the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) lies 5 m below \(O\) and 4 mm from the axis of the bar. We calculate the inverse matrix of the deformation gradient at \(P\) with a computer, and how to calculate it by hand we will see in chapter 2:

\[\mat F^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}999998048004 & 4{,}684794 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ -4{,}684794 \cdot 10^{-10} & 1{,}000000585600 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1{,}000000585600 \end{bmatrix} .\]

That it really is the inverse we check by multiplication, \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^{-1}\mat F = \mat I\). Let us calculate the entry \(xx\) of the product \(\mat F\mat F^{-1}\) by hand: row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F\) is \((1{,}000001952,\ -4{,}6848 \cdot 10^{-10},\ 0)\) and column \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) is \((0{,}999998048004,\ -4{,}684794 \cdot 10^{-10},\ 0)\), so

\[\begin{aligned} &1{,}000001952 \cdot 0{,}999998048004 \\ &\quad + (-4{,}6848 \cdot 10^{-10}) \cdot (-4{,}684794 \cdot 10^{-10}) + 0 = 1{,}000000000000 \end{aligned}\]

to twelve decimal places. By (1.57) we get

\[\mat E^* = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}951994 \cdot 10^{-6} & 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} & 0 \\ 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} & -5{,}856005 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856005 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

The Green-Lagrange tensor at \(P\) has \(1{,}952002 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and twice \(-5{,}855998 \cdot 10^{-7}\) on the diagonal, the small strain tensor \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and twice \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\) (sections 1.17.2 and 1.17.3). Rounded to five significant digits, the diagonal entries of all three matrices are equal, and the entries off the diagonal differ by at most \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-15}\). The largest difference, between \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\), is \(7{,}6 \cdot 10^{-12}\), about four millionths of the entry.

The differences on the diagonal have a simple pattern. For the entry \(xx\), \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12} = \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -5{,}715 \cdot 10^{-12} = -\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\), and for the entry \(yy\) likewise \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 = 1{,}71 \cdot 10^{-13}\) and \(-\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 = -5{,}14 \cdot 10^{-13}\). Why? A short fibre along the axis \(x\) leans only by the ratio \(4{,}7 \cdot 10^{-10}\), so it lies almost along the axis \(x\) both before and after loading, and the formulas for the bar hold for it, as the curves near \(L_1/L_0 = 1\) show. The Green-Lagrange strain is \(\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), and the new quotient, by step 4 of the derivation of the formula (1.56), almost \(\varepsilon - \tfrac32\,\varepsilon^2\). So we check the entry \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\) also without a computer:

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 &= 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - \tfrac32\,(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6})^2 \\ &= 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - 5{,}715 \cdot 10^{-12} \\ &= 1{,}951994 \cdot 10^{-6} , \end{aligned}\]

which, on the digits shown, is the entry from the computer. The entries \(E_{\mathrm{xy}} = -5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xy}} = 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16}\) even have opposite signs. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(H_{\mathrm{xy}} + H_{\mathrm{yx}}) = \tfrac12\,(-4{,}6848 \cdot 10^{-10} + 4{,}6848 \cdot 10^{-10}) = 0\), both consist only of products of partial derivatives. For \(E_{\mathrm{xy}}\) they are given by (1.48):

\[\begin{aligned} E_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} + \tfrac12\,\big(H_{\mathrm{xx}}\,H_{\mathrm{xy}} + H_{\mathrm{yx}}\,H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zx}}\,H_{\mathrm{zy}}\big) \\ &= 0 + \tfrac12\,\big(-9{,}145 \cdot 10^{-16} - 2{,}743 \cdot 10^{-16} + 0\big) = -5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} . \end{aligned}\]

In \(\mat E^*\) the same sum of products appears with the opposite sign, \(-\tfrac12\) instead of \(\tfrac12\), and also the products \((\mat H\mat H)_{\mathrm{xy}} + (\mat H\mat H)_{\mathrm{yx}}\), which are subtracted here, as we will see in step 5 of the proof of corollary 1.122 below. So \(E^*_{\mathrm{xy}} = 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16}\). On the diagonal, too, products appear with the other coefficients, \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) and \(-\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\).

Let us also test theorem 1.120 on the bar. For the fibre in the direction \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\) of section 1.17.2, \(A = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = -3{,}036443 \cdot 10^{-7}\), less than \(G = -3{,}036441 \cdot 10^{-7}\) by \(2GA = 1{,}84 \cdot 10^{-13}\). The quotient \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\), calculated exactly from the field (1.18), comes within \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-11}\) and \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-12}\) of the value \(A\) for fibres of length 1 mm and 0.1 mm, as the theorem says.

For small partial derivatives the matrices \(\mat E^*\), \(\mat E\) and \(\ten\varepsilon\) therefore differ only by terms with products of partial derivatives, and then we need not distinguish whether we give points and directions of fibres before loading or after it (CM §3.5.1, PDF p. 141, BOWER §2.1.7, PDF p. 50). For a single fibre we showed this exactly with the relation \(G - A = 2GA\). For all entries of the matrices at once, though, we want to show more: that the entries of the matrices \(\mat E\), \(\mat E^*\) and \(\ten\varepsilon\) differ by at most a fixed number times the square of the largest partial derivative (corollary 1.122 below). For \(\mat E - \ten\varepsilon\) this follows from \(\mat E = \ten\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\). The matrix \(\mat E^*\), however, contains \(\mat F^{-1}\), so we also need a bound for the entries of the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\).

How close is \(\mat F^{-1}\) to the matrix \(\mat I - \mat H\)? For the sheared cube \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) exactly, because \(\mat K\mat K = \mat 0\) (section 1.16.5, figure 1.373, top). For the hanging bar the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\), which we computed with a computer, differs from the matrix \(\mat I - \mat H\) by at most \(3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\), in the entry \(xx\). This is the square of the largest partial derivative, \((1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6})^2 = 3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\). Why? We can express the difference \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\) from the equation \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat I\), and we get \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\). If \(\mat B\) is small, then \(\mat H\mat B\) is a product of two small matrices, and \(\mat B\) is almost \(\mat H\). The difference \(\mat F^{-1} - (\mat I - \mat H) = \mat H - \mat B = \mat H\mat B\) is therefore almost \(\mat H\mat H\), whose entry \(xx\) we calculate by hand:

\[H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + H_{\mathrm{xy}}\,H_{\mathrm{yx}} + H_{\mathrm{xz}}\,H_{\mathrm{zx}} = 3{,}810 \cdot 10^{-12} - 2{,}2 \cdot 10^{-19} + 0 = 3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12} .\]

This is the number from the computer. That \(\mat B\) really is small, the same equation tells us when we read it as an inequality for the largest entry of the matrix \(\mat B\). As in section 1.17.3, let \(m\) be a number that no partial derivative of the displacement at the point exceeds in absolute value. The lemma that follows also requires \(m \le \tfrac16\). We need this condition in its proof, where we divide by the number \(1 - 3m\), which must be positive and not too small: for \(m \le \tfrac16\) it is at least \(\tfrac12\).

Lemma 1.121 Estimate of the inverse matrix (ocena inverzne matrike)

Let \(\mat H\) be a \(3 \times 3\) matrix and \(m\) a number with \(0 < m \le \tfrac16\) such that \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m\) for all indices \(i\) and \(j\). Let the matrix \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) have an inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\), and let \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\). Then

\[\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B , \qquad \mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat H + \mat H\mat B , \tag{1.61}\]

and for all \(i\) and \(j\) we have \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 2m\) and \(|(\mat H\mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 6m^2\).

Proof

We must show both equalities and both estimates. We get the equalities from the definition of the inverse matrix, the estimate for \(\mat B\) from the first equality, read as an inequality, and the estimate for \(\mat H\mat B\) from the estimate for \(\mat B\).

  1. By definition 1.107 of the inverse matrix, \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat I\). We substitute \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) and \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat B\). By item 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product and by lemma 1.106 on multiplication by the identity matrix, \((\mat I + \mat H)(\mat I - \mat B) = \mat I - \mat B + \mat H - \mat H\mat B\).
  2. This matrix is \(\mat I\), so by the calculation rules for matrices (lemma 1.95) \(\mat H - \mat B - \mat H\mat B = \mat 0\), hence \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\). This is the first equality.
  3. From \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat B\) and the first equality it follows that \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat H + \mat H\mat B\), the second equality.

Let us draw what steps 4 and 5 estimate. At the top are the nine numbers \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}|\), the absolute values of the entries of the matrix \(\mat B\), and at the bottom the entry \((y, z)\) of the product \(\mat H\mat B\) as an example of an arbitrary entry \((i, j)\).

  1. Let \(\mu\) be the largest of the nine numbers \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}|\). Among finitely many numbers one is the largest, in the figure circled in orange, and each of the nine is at most \(\mu\).
  2. By the first equality, \(B_{\mathrm{ij}} = H_{\mathrm{ij}} - \sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ik}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\), where the sum multiplies row \(\ix{i}\) of the matrix \(\mat H\) by column \(\ix{j}\) of the matrix \(\mat B\), in blue in the figure. By the triangle inequality for numbers and the rule for the absolute value of a product (lemma 1.6), \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le |H_{\mathrm{ij}}| + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} |H_{\mathrm{ik}}|\,|B_{\mathrm{kj}}| \le m + 3m\mu\), because the sum has three terms and each is at most \(m\mu\).
  3. The inequality from step 5 holds for all entries, also for the entry with \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| = \mu\). So \(\mu \le m + 3m\mu\), hence \((1 - 3m)\,\mu \le m\).

Let us draw by what number we will divide in step 7. The horizontal axis is the number \(m\), the marks \(\tfrac16\) and \(\tfrac13\) are the important ones. The vertical axis is the value \(1/(1 - 3m)\). The orange curve shows this value. It grows because the denominator \(1 - 3m\) gets smaller as \(m\) grows. The dot at \(m = \tfrac16\) has the value \(2\), which the grey horizontal line also shows. For a smaller \(m\) the value is smaller than \(2\). The grey vertical line at \(m = \tfrac13\) is the place where the denominator becomes zero, that is, where the value is no longer bounded.

  1. Since \(m \le \tfrac16\), we have \(1 - 3m \ge \tfrac12\), so \(1/(1 - 3m) \le 2\), as the dot shows. When we divide the inequality by the positive number \(1 - 3m\), we get \(\mu \le m/(1 - 3m) \le 2m\). So \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 2m\) for all \(i\) and \(j\).
  2. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat H\mat B\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ik}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three terms, of which each is at most \(m \cdot 2m\) in absolute value, because \(\mu \le 2m\) in the estimate in the figure. By the triangle inequality for numbers, therefore, \(|(\mat H\mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 6m^2\).

Source: LEBL2 prop. 8.2.6 (PDF pp. 23-24) proves the related statement that a matrix close enough to an invertible matrix is invertible too. The lemma and the proof are not from the source.

The lemma says that \(\mat F^{-1}\) equals \(\mat I - \mat H\) up to the matrix \(\mat H\mat B\), whose entries are at most \(6m^2\). The proof used the equation \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\) twice: first as an inequality that bounds the largest entry of \(\mat B\), then to estimate the correction \(\mat H\mat B\). We needed the condition \(m \le \tfrac16\) in step 7, so that the number \(1 - 3m\) is positive and not too small (it is at least \(\tfrac12\), so \(1/(1 - 3m) \le 2\)). The lemma does not prove that \(\mat F^{-1}\) exists but assumes it, like this whole section. For the cube \(m = 0{,}001\), \(\mat B = \mat K\) and \(\mat H\mat B = \mat K\mat K = \mat 0\). For the hanging bar \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the largest entry of \(\mat B\) is \(1{,}951996 \cdot 10^{-6}\), less than \(2m\), and the largest entry of \(\mat H\mat B\) is \(3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\), below the bound \(6m^2 = 2{,}29 \cdot 10^{-11}\). Now we can compare all three measures.

Corollary 1.122 Three strain measures for small partial derivatives (tri mere deformacije pri majhnih parcialnih odvodih)

Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient at an interior point of a body and \(m > 0\) a number such that \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m\) for all \(i\) and \(j\). Let \(\mat E\) and \(\ten\varepsilon\) be the Green-Lagrange strain tensor and the small strain tensor at this point. Then for all \(i\) and \(j\) the first estimate below holds. If in addition \(m \le \tfrac16\) and the deformation gradient \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) has an inverse matrix, then for the Euler-Almansi strain tensor \(\mat E^*\) at this point the other two estimates also hold:

\[\begin{aligned} |E_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le \tfrac32\,m^2 , \\ |E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le 12\,m^2 , \\ |E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le \tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2 . \end{aligned} \tag{1.62}\]
Proof

We must show three estimates. We write each difference with products of matrices. We bound the first only by \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m\), and the other two by lemma 1.121 on the estimate of the inverse matrix, which requires \(m \le \tfrac16\).

  1. By lemma 1.113 on the Green-Lagrange strain from the displacement gradient, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T + \mat H^\T\mat H)\), and by (1.51), \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\). So \(\mat E - \ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\).
  2. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat H^\T\mat H\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three products, each at most \(m^2\) in absolute value. By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6), therefore, \(|E_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le \tfrac12 \cdot 3m^2 = \tfrac32\,m^2\).
  3. Let \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\) as in lemma 1.121. By item 2 of lemma 1.101 on transposing a sum, a multiple and a product, and since the identity matrix equals its transpose, \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat I - \mat B)^\T = \mat I - \mat B^\T\).
  4. By item 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product and lemma 1.106 on multiplication by the identity matrix, \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = (\mat I - \mat B^\T)(\mat I - \mat B) = \mat I - \mat B - \mat B^\T + \mat B^\T\mat B\). By (1.57), therefore, \(\mat E^* = \tfrac12(\mat B + \mat B^\T - \mat B^\T\mat B)\), as for the cube, where \(\mat B = \mat K\).
  5. By lemma 1.121, \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\), and by item 2 of lemma 1.101, \(\mat B^\T = \mat H^\T - (\mat H\mat B)^\T\). Inserting this into step 4 and subtracting \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) gives
    \[\mat E^* - \ten\varepsilon = -\tfrac12\big(\mat H\mat B + (\mat H\mat B)^\T + \mat B^\T\mat B\big) .\]
  6. By lemma 1.121 every entry of the matrices \(\mat H\mat B\) and \((\mat H\mat B)^\T\) is at most \(6m^2\) in absolute value. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat B^\T\mat B\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} B_{\mathrm{ki}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three products, each at most \(2m \cdot 2m = 4m^2\) by the same lemma, so it is at most \(12m^2\). By the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le \tfrac12\,(6m^2 + 6m^2 + 12m^2) = 12m^2\).
  7. We write the difference as \(E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}} = (E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}) + (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}})\). By the triangle inequality for numbers and steps 6 and 2, \(|E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 12m^2 + \tfrac32\,m^2 = \tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2\).

Source: CM §3.5.1 (PDF pp. 140-141) says that for small partial derivatives, when terms of the order of the square are dropped, the Green-Lagrange and the Eulerian strain tensor need not be distinguished. BOWER §2.1.7 (PDF p. 50) says that the infinitesimal strain approximates the Lagrange strain, and the Eulerian strain with the same accuracy, and leaves the latter to the reader. The estimates with fixed numbers and the proof are not from the sources.

The figure has three panels, each with its own horizontal axis, on which every gap between powers is a factor of \(10\) (a logarithmic scale). On such an axis the distance between two points does not tell the difference of the numbers but their ratio: a point one gap further to the right is at a number ten times larger. Each has three rows for the differences between the measures: \(E - \varepsilon\), \(E^* - \varepsilon\) and \(E^* - E\). Every row is built in the same way. The blackwhite dot is the true difference, that is, the largest entry of the difference of the two measures. The blue dash is the bound from corollary 1.122. The dot always lies to the left of the dash or on it, because the true difference does not exceed the bound. The grey dimension between them says how many times the bound is larger than the true difference: a dimension one gap between powers long means ten times.

The top panel is the sheared cube with \(m = 0{,}001\), the middle one is the hanging bar at the point \(P\) with \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\). Each panel has its own powers on the axis: the axis of the bar and the axis of the last panel have different ones, because the differences for the bar are much smaller, and for the last panel much larger. For the cube the largest entries of the differences, \(zz\), are taken, for the bar \(xx\). The last panel is the matrix with all nine entries \(-\tfrac16\) at \(m = \tfrac16\). For it all three differences equal the bounds, so there are no grey dimensions and the dots lie on the dashes.

The corollary says exactly what we saw on the numbers. For small partial derivatives the entries of all three matrices differ by at most a fixed number times the square of the largest partial derivative. For steel, where \(m\) is of the order \(0{,}001\), the differences are at most of the order \(10^{-5}\), a hundred times less than the partial derivatives themselves. The numbers \(\tfrac32\), \(12\) and \(\tfrac{27}{2}\) are the bounds that the proof gives, and with the same assumptions they cannot be made smaller. This is shown by the matrix \(\mat H\) with all nine entries equal to \(-\tfrac16\), at \(m = \tfrac16\). We start the calculation with the matrix \(\mat J\) with all nine entries equal to \(1\). Then \(\mat H = -\tfrac16\,\mat J\). Every entry of the matrix \(\mat J\mat J\) is a sum of three products \(1 \cdot 1\), so \(\mat J\mat J = 3\,\mat J\), and \(\mat J\) is symmetric. With this one rule we get all the matrices:

\[\begin{aligned} \mat F &= \mat I - \tfrac16\,\mat J , \qquad \mat F^{-1} = \mat I + \tfrac13\,\mat J , \qquad \mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1} = -\tfrac13\,\mat J , \\ \mat H\mat B &= \tfrac1{18}\,\mat J\mat J = \tfrac16\,\mat J , \qquad \mat E - \ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H = \tfrac1{72}\,\mat J\mat J = \tfrac1{24}\,\mat J , \\ \mat E^* - \ten\varepsilon &= -\tfrac12\big(\mat H\mat B + (\mat H\mat B)^\T + \mat B^\T\mat B\big) = -\tfrac12\big(\tfrac16 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac13\big)\,\mat J = -\tfrac13\,\mat J , \\ \mat E^* - \mat E &= -\tfrac13\,\mat J - \tfrac1{24}\,\mat J = -\tfrac38\,\mat J . \end{aligned}\]

For \(\mat E^* - \ten\varepsilon\) we used step 5 of the proof of the corollary and \(\mat B^\T\mat B = \tfrac19\,\mat J\mat J = \tfrac13\,\mat J\). That \(\mat F^{-1}\) is the right one, we check by multiplying:

\[\big(\mat I - \tfrac16\,\mat J\big)\big(\mat I + \tfrac13\,\mat J\big) = \mat I + \tfrac13\,\mat J - \tfrac16\,\mat J - \tfrac1{18}\,\mat J\mat J = \mat I + \tfrac16\,\mat J - \tfrac16\,\mat J = \mat I .\]

So the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) has \(1 + \tfrac13 = \tfrac43\) on the diagonal and \(\tfrac13\) off it. All the matrices of lemma 1.121 on the estimate of the inverse matrix and of the corollary have nine equal entries each:

matrix each of its entries bound
\(\mat B\) \(-\tfrac13\) \(2m = \tfrac13\)
\(\mat H\mat B\) \(\tfrac16\) \(6m^2 = \tfrac16\)
\(\mat E - \ten\varepsilon\) \(\tfrac1{24}\) \(\tfrac32\,m^2 = \tfrac1{24}\)
\(\mat E^* - \ten\varepsilon\) \(-\tfrac13\) \(12\,m^2 = \tfrac13\)
\(\mat E^* - \mat E\) \(-\tfrac38\) \(\tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2 = \tfrac38\)

All three bounds are attained exactly at the matrix with all entries \(-\tfrac16\), which we also checked with SymPy: its dots lie on the blue dashes. The first bound is attained for every \(m\): if all nine entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) equal \(m\), every entry of the matrix \(\tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\) equals \(\tfrac12 \cdot 3m^2 = \tfrac32\,m^2\). In both examples below the actual differences are smaller than the bounds, about three times for the first estimate and at least six times for the other two.

  • The sheared cube, \(m = 0{,}001\): the bounds are \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\), \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-5}\) and \(1{,}35 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The largest differences are in the entry \(zz\), \(E_{\mathrm{zz}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}} - E_{\mathrm{zz}} = -10^{-6}\).
  • The hanging bar at the point \(P\), \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\): the bounds are \(5{,}7 \cdot 10^{-12}\), \(4{,}6 \cdot 10^{-11}\) and \(5{,}1 \cdot 10^{-11}\). The largest differences are in the entry \(xx\), \(1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12}\), \(-5{,}715 \cdot 10^{-12}\) and \(-7{,}6 \cdot 10^{-12}\).

But what if the partial derivatives are not small? Then we must not use the corollary, and the three measures are no longer almost equal. Let us stretch the bar to twice its length along the axis \(x\), and later we will compress it to a fifth of its length.

Let us draw the bars at a wall, so that only the change of length is seen. The hatched line is the wall from which we measure. The blackwhite bar is before loading, its length is \(L_0\). The orange bar, twice as long, is stretched to the length \(L_1 = 2L_0\). The lower orange bar is compressed to a fifth, its length is \(L_1 = L_0/5\). All three are drawn to the same scale.

For the double length let us write the matrices on the board:

\[\mat F = \mathrm{diag}(2, 1, 1) , \qquad \mat H = \mathrm{diag}(1, 0, 0) , \qquad \mat F^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(\tfrac12, 1, 1) .\]

The largest entry of the matrix \(\mat H\) is \(m = 1 > \tfrac16\), and the matrix \(\mat F\) has an inverse matrix. All three measures in the entry \(xx\):

measure formula value
small strain tensor \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = H_{\mathrm{xx}}\) \(1\)
Green-Lagrange tensor, lemma 1.113 \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,(2H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2) = \tfrac12\,(2^2 - 1)\) \(1{,}5\)
Euler-Almansi tensor, (1.57) \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,(1 - 1/2^2)\) \(0{,}375\)

The number \(2^2\) is the square of the length ratio \(2\) along the axis \(x\). In figure 1.413 these are the dots at \(L_1/L_0 = 2\). The measures differ: \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is larger than \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by a factor of \(1{,}5\) and larger than \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by a factor of \(4\).

Why so strongly? The reason is in the denominator. Let \(L\) be the length of the bar before loading and \(l\) after it. Both measures divide the same difference of the squares of lengths, but by different numbers:

\[E_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{l^2 - L^2}{2L^2} , \qquad E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{l^2 - L^2}{2l^2} .\]
