For \(l = 2L\) the second denominator is four times the first, while for \(l\) barely larger than \(L\) the two denominators are almost equal. \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) differs from the small strain tensor by \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\). Here this is \(0{,}5\), half of the strain itself, while for \(H_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}001\) it is \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), two thousand times less than the strain.

What does corollary 1.122 say here? The first estimate does not need the condition \(m \le \tfrac16\), and indeed \(|E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}| = 0{,}5 \le \tfrac32\,m^2 = 1{,}5\). But this bound is larger than the strain itself, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\), so it does not say that the measures are almost equal. At \(m = 1\) the corollary does not guarantee the other two estimates.

Would the other two estimates hold for a larger \(m\) as well? We have not proved this, and in general they do not hold. Let us compress the bar to a fifth of its length. Then \(\mat F = \mathrm{diag}(\tfrac15, 1, 1)\), \(\mat H = \mathrm{diag}(-\tfrac45, 0, 0)\) and \(m = \tfrac45\), and the matrix \(\mat F\) has the inverse matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(5, 1, 1)\). In the entry \(xx\) we have

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}8 , \qquad E_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\big((\tfrac15)^2 - 1\big) = -0{,}48 , \qquad E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,(1 - 5^2) = -12 .\]

The first estimate holds, \(|E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}| = 0{,}32 \le \tfrac32\,m^2 = 0{,}96\). The second does not: \(|E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}| = 11{,}2\), while the bound is \(12\,m^2 = 7{,}68\). The third does not either: \(|E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - E_{\mathrm{xx}}| = 11{,}52\), while the bound is \(\tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2 = 8{,}64\). Without a condition on \(m\) the corollary therefore does not hold. Whether \(\tfrac16\) is the largest bound at which it still holds, we have not investigated. We chose the condition so that the proof in step 7 of lemma 1.121 works. Rubber can be stretched to twice its length, so for it the choice of the measure is not a matter of indifference.

Both examples in an overview, with the bounds from the corollary. The bound \(\tfrac32\,m^2\) may be used for every \(m\). The bound \(12\,m^2\) is guaranteed by the corollary only for \(m \le \tfrac16\), which neither of the two examples satisfies, so it is in the last column only for comparison:

| length ratio \(L_1/L_0\) | \(m\) | \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) | \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) | \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\) | \(\lvert E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\rvert\), bound \(\tfrac32\,m^2\) | \(\lvert E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\rvert\), bound \(12\,m^2\) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | \(2\) | \(1\) | \(1\) | \(1{,}5\) | \(0{,}375\) | \(0{,}5 \le 1{,}5\) | \(0{,}625 \le 12\) | | \(\tfrac15\) | \(\tfrac45\) | \(-0{,}8\) | \(-0{,}48\) | \(-12\) | \(0{,}32 \le 0{,}96\) | \(11{,}2 > 7{,}68\) |

So in steel structures we use the small strain tensor, where the measures almost agree, while for large strains, for example in rubber, we must say which measure we use and whether the direction of the fibre is given before loading or after it.

Three measures together:

measure the fibre is given the change of the square of the length is divided by
Green-Lagrange tensor \(\mat E\) before loading, by the direction \(\vek n\) \(2L_0^2\)
Euler-Almansi tensor \(\mat E^*\) after loading, by the direction \(\vek m\) \(2L_1^2\)
small strain tensor \(\ten\varepsilon\) before or after loading \(2L_0^2 \approx 2L_1^2\)

We can now calculate from the displacement field the strain at every interior point and in every direction. The Green-Lagrange tensor gives it exactly when we give the direction of the fibre before loading, and the Euler-Almansi tensor when we give it after loading, while for small partial derivatives the small strain tensor is enough. The path went from displacements to strains. Often we must go the other way: we know the six components of strain and look for the displacements. Is this always possible? We calculate six components from only three components of the displacement, so they cannot be arbitrary. Which conditions they must satisfy, we look at in the next section.
